ABOOT: This word is a humorous (though incorrect) take on the Canadian accent saying the word “about”.
ACORN: After the decisive Battle of Vimy Ridge during the First World War, Canadian soldier, Lieutenant Leslie Miller, gathered acorns from oak trees amongst the rubble and wreckage. Miller brought the acorns back home to Scarborough, Ontario and planted the trees as a legacy to those who perished. The acorns from those trees were then repatriated and planted back in France in 2018. Lieutenant Leslie Miller's Vimy Oaks are now growing on Vimy Ridge, and today approximately 1,000 descendant Vimy Oaks have been planted across Canada as commemorative trees. Check out the [Vimy Oaks Legacy](https://vimyoakslegacy.ca/) website to learn more!
ACTOR: Canada is home to some incredible actors! Some of our all-time favourites include: Mike Myers, Rachel McAdams, Jim Carrey, Seth Rogen, Ryan Reynolds, Graham Greene, Ryan Gosling, Cobie Smulders, John Candy, Elliot Page, Keanu Reeves, Simu Liu, Neve Campbell, Sarah Polley, Hayden Christensen, Donald & Kiefer Sutherland, Michael J. Fox, Tom Green, Evangeline Lilly, Jay Baruchel, Michael Cera, William Shatner, Brendan Fraser, Nathan Fillion, Catherine O'Hara, Eugene & Dan Levy, Leslie Nielsen, Martin Short, Gordon Pinsent, Megan Follows, Christopher Plummer, Lorne Greene, Adam Beach, Dan Aykroyd, Sandra Oh, and Matthew Perry just to name a few! April 19th is the 10th annual [National Canadian Film Day](https://canfilmday.ca/)! You're invited to an All You Can Watch Buffet of Canadian film, featuring Canadian actors, directors, producers, and more. Head over to [canfilmday.ca](https://canfilmday.ca/) to check out all the films! #CanFilmDay
ALARM: Robert Foulis is known as the inventor of the world's first steam-operated fog alarm, which was installed on Partridge Island in the Bay of Fundy in 1859, just off the coast of Saint John, New Brunswick. While Foulis never patented or even profited from his life-saving innovation, his steam foghorn invention assisted fogbound mariners for over a century.
ALBUM: The Juno Award for [Album of the Year](https://junoawards.ca/nomination/2024-album-of-the-year-charlotte-cardin/) is an annual award presented by the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences for the best album released in Canada. It has been awarded since 1975. Arcade Fire, Celine Dion, Michael Bublé and The Weeknd are the artists with the most wins in this category with three each; Dion is the most nominated artist with 12 nominations.
ALERT: Alert, in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut, Canada, is the northernmost continuously inhabited place in the world, on Ellesmere Island (Queen Elizabeth Islands) just 817 kilometres from the North Pole. Alert was named after HMS Alert, a British ship that wintered in the area from 1875-76.
ALLEY: Each spring along the eastern coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, it's prime time for spotting icebergs. With many little towns along a thousand kilometres of coastline, this area known as "Iceberg Alley" is an outstanding location for viewing roving blue natural ice sculptures that float down from Greenland and Canada's Arctic. The massive chunks of broken glaciers are only 10% visible since most of the iceberg is submerged and floating on its side.
ANTHEM: Canada’s national anthem, O Canada, was first performed in 1880 in Québec City and has since become a defining part of our shared identity. Originally written in French, an English version followed in 1906, with its lyrics continuing to evolve for more than a century. In 1980, Canada’s National Anthem Act received royal assent and officially took effect on July 1, becoming a centerpiece of that year’s Dominion Day celebrations. Whether sung in schools, at hockey games, or during national ceremonies, O Canada remains a moment that unites Canadians from coast to coast to coast.
ANVIL: Anvil is a Canadian heavy metal band formed in Toronto in 1978. The band currently consists of founding members guitarist/vocalist Steve "Lips" Kudlow and drummer Robb Reiner, along with bassist Chris Robertson who joined in 2014. As of 2022, the band has released nineteen studio albums; they have been cited as having influenced many notable heavy metal groups including Megadeth, Slayer, Anthrax, and Metallica.
ARMED: Canadian Armed Forces Day takes place on the first Sunday in June each year and is a celebration of the members of the [Canadian Armed Forces](https://forces.ca/), both those who are currently serving and those who have served in the past. To all current and past members of the Canadian Armed Forces, and to the loved ones who stand with you, we appreciate and recognize your bravery, dedication and sacrifice. Thank you for answering the call to serve, and for making Canada and the world a better place to live.
ARROW: Canada's response to the threat of Soviet nuclear bombers was the Avro Arrow. A marvel of engineering, it was a twin-engine, all-weather supersonic interceptor. Only five Avro Arrow planes were ever built, yet this innovative jet fighter put Canada on top of the aviation world in the 1950s.
AWARD: The 2023 Juno Awards took place in Edmonton, Alberta last night! The annual awards ceremony celebrates outstanding achievements in Canadian music. The Juno Awards began in 1964 as the RPM Gold Leaf Awards, and in 1971 they were renamed the Juno Awards after the Roman goddess and in tribute to Pierre Juneau, the first chairperson of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) who was responsible for introducing the Canadian content quota to Canadian radio that year.
AXIOM: An axiom is a basic rule accepted as true without needing proof, and it’s where all logical thinking begins. World Logic Day on January 14 celebrates these foundational ideas, the same way games like Canuckle and Canoku start with simple rules that guide every word guess and emoji placement. From letters to patterns, great puzzles are built one solid axiom at a time.
AZURE: The word azure means bright sky-blue, a colour seen across Canada’s vast skies and lakes. In heraldry, azure also appears in [The Coat of Arms of Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/official-symbols-canada.html#a1) on the shield, representing the royal emblems of Ireland (a harp) and France (three fleurs-de-lis). Together with symbols from England and Scotland, these elements reflect the historical nations that shaped Canada’s founding.
BADGE: On Canadian Armed Forces Day (celebrated on the first Sunday in June), we recognize the dedication and service of Canada's military personnel. In the Canadian Armed Forces, a badge carries deep meaning - reflecting a unit's identity, honouring its history, and building pride among those who wear it. From regimental crests to specialized qualification badges, each one tells a story of dedication and service to Canada. Many incorporate iconic symbols like maple leaves, beavers, or crowns, proudly connecting each badge to Canada's heritage.
BALER: Balers have played a significant role in Canadian history, particularly in the development of the Prairie provinces. The ability to compress and transport hay and straw efficiently helped to open up new land for agriculture and settlement. The Canadian agricultural industry relies heavily on balers, with many farmers using them to harvest and process crops like wheat, barley, oats, and alfalfa.
BALSA: Balsa wood is lightweight yet incredibly strong, making it a go-to material for Canadian crafters and hobbyists! Native to South America, balsa is used in model airplanes, ping pong paddles, and even surfboards. Many Canadian builders appreciate its ease of use and buoyancy, making it perfect for crafting floatable objects. So next time you spot a model plane or a small raft in Canada, there's a good chance balsa wood is behind the design!
BARGE: The McBarge, officially named the Friendship 500, was a floating McDonald's restaurant built for Expo 86 in Vancouver. This sleek, futuristic barge served Big Macs with a waterfront view, but after the fair, it was left adrift, moving from site to site along the B.C. coast. Despite hopes for restoration, the McBarge met a sad fate in March 2025 when it sank near Maple Ridge. While its golden arches faded, its legend lives on as one of Canada's most unique fast-food relics.
BARON: Anyone outside of Western Canada might not know or understand the cult following behind the unassuming [Burger Baron](https://burgerbaronedmonton.com/) restaurant. The popular fast-food chain, with its distinctive sign, popular mushroom burger and 25 locations around Alberta, has been a part of the Prairie dining scene since the 1950s. Founded in 1957 in either Calgary or Lethbridge, Alberta (the location and ownership of the first site is disputed), Burger Baron was one of the first drive-in restaurant chains in Western Canada. Many of the owners are Lebanese Canadians, connected to Rudy Kemaldean of Edmonton. Among other things, Burger Baron is famous for being endorsed by former Edmonton Oilers hockey coach Glen Sather and other former members of the Edmonton Oilers.
BATON: Canada has a strong tradition of excellence in relay races, with its teams achieving notable success on the world stage. The Canadian men's 4x100m relay team famously won gold at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, a triumph that echoed the country's prowess in track and field. More recently, the men's 4x100m team clinched silver at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, further solidifying Canada's status as a powerhouse in relay events. These achievements highlight the strength and teamwork that define [Canadian athletics](https://olympic.ca/sports/athletics/).
BEADS: Beading has a very long artistic and cultural history among the Indigenous people in Canada. At least 8,000 years before Europeans came to Canada, First Nations people were using beads in elaborate designs and for trade. Today, you can find beautiful First Nations beadwork at powwows, First Nations arts stores and museums across Canada. June 21st is National Indigenous Peoples Day. Take the opportunity to learn more about the cultural and linguistic diversity as well as the contributions of First Nations, Inuit and Métis Peoples.
BEAKS: Atlantic puffins along Canada’s eastern coasts are known for their large, brightly coloured beaks, which shift from dull grey in winter to vibrant orange and yellow during the summer breeding season. Each year, they shed the outer colourful layer of their bill. These specialized beaks also feature tiny spines and notched edges, allowing puffins to hold multiple fish at once, sometimes dozens, making them remarkably efficient hunters in Atlantic waters.
BEAVER: The beaver is one of Canada's most iconic animals! Once vital to the fur trade that shaped the country's early history, it became a national symbol of industry and perseverance. In 1975, the beaver was officially recognized as Canada's national animal. You can even spot this hardworking rodent on the Canadian nickel!
BEETS: Sugar beets have played a key role in Canada's sugar production for over a century! While most of Canada's sugar comes from imported cane, sugar beets are grown domestically - mainly in Alberta. In the town of Taber, home to Canada's last remaining sugar beet processing plant, 200 local farm families supply the refinery with approximately 840,000 tonnes of sugar beets each year. This yields 125,000 tonnes of sugar, making up 8–10% of Canada's total sugar consumption! From root to sweet treat, these beets keep Canada's sugar industry thriving!
BELTS: Wampum are tubular purple and white beads made from shells. Wampum are used primarily by Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands for ornamental, ceremonial, diplomatic and commercial purposes. Belts made of wampum were used to mark agreements between peoples. Wampum belts and other wampum bead artifacts continue to hold significance for Indigenous peoples and any treaties or agreements they might represent.
BENCH: In the House of Commons, MPs with leadership roles sit on the front bench, while everyone else sits on the back bench. Backbenchers may not wear the cabinet title, but they’re far from idle, reviewing legislation in committees, introducing private members’ bills, and taking part in Question Period. In the 45th Canadian Parliament, all 343 MPs, including the backbench, keep the work of democracy moving every day.
BICEP: Canadian arm wrestling legend Devon Larratt is known around the world for his powerful biceps and unmatched technique! Born in Victoria, British Columbia, Larratt served in the Canadian Armed Forces before becoming a dominant force in professional arm wrestling. With multiple world titles and viral matchups under his belt, he's helped put Canada on the map in this intense sport of strength and strategy.
BINGO: The game of Bingo has been a beloved pastime in Canada for decades! In fact, the first official Canadian Bingo hall opened in the 1940s in British Columbia, and the game quickly became a popular way to raise money for charities, schools, and local communities. Whether played at a community centre or as a family game night favourite, Bingo remains a fun way to bring Canadians together! From coast to coast, Canadians have enjoyed shouting "Bingo!" as a way to win big and support their communities at the same time.
BIOME: The five main Canadian biomes are tundra, boreal forest, grassland, temperate deciduous forest, and mountain forest. The boreal forest or taiga is the largest biome in Canada.
BITES: [History Bites](https://historybites.ca/) is a Canadian television series on the History Television network that ran from 1998 to 2004. Created by Rick Green, the sketch comedy show explored what would be on television if the medium was around for 5,000 years of human history. The show featured a large ensemble cast. It earned five Gemini nominations and won a Canadian Comedy Award.
BLADE: Today marks the start of the [Western Hockey League](https://chl.ca/whl/) (WHL) regular season in Canada! The [Saskatoon Blades](https://chl.ca/whl-blades/) are a Canadian major junior ice hockey team based in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Founded in 1964, the Blades were a charter team of the then-Western Canada Junior Hockey League in 1966, and are the only club that has played every season in the league in its original location. The team has twice hosted the Memorial Cup tournament, in 1989 and in 2013.
BLAME: "Blame Canada" is a satirical song from the 1999 animated film South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut, written by Trey Parker and Marc Shaiman. The song was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 72nd Academy Awards. "Blame Canada" has become a catch phrase for shifting attention away from a problem or serious social issue by humorously laying responsibility on Canada.
BLAND: Despite the name, Blanding’s turtles aren’t bland at all! This bright-eyed freshwater species, found in southern Ontario, Quebec, and parts of the Maritimes, has a striking yellow throat and domed shell. Sadly, these turtles are endangered, and conservation efforts across Canada are helping protect their wetlands and nesting sites so they can continue to thrive.
BLAZE: In Canada's vast wilderness, a blaze isn't just a fiery flash - it's also a mark on a tree used to guide hikers along a trail! Trail blazes, often painted or carved, help outdoor adventurers find their way through forests, mountains, and national parks across the country. The tradition of blazing trails goes back centuries, including by Indigenous Peoples who navigated the land with deep knowledge and skill.
BLIND: In response to rising blindness rates caused by the Halifax explosion and veterans returning home from World War I, the [Canadian National Institute for the Blind](https://www.cnib.ca/) (CNIB) was founded and incorporated by a group of seven Canadian men - several veterans and blind men among them. Since the founding in 1918, the CNIB Foundation has been creating programs, providing services and advocating to change the lives of Canadians who are blind or partially sighted. CNIB is a non-profit organization driven to change what it is to be blind today.
BLOOD: This week is National Blood Donor Week and today is World Blood Donor Day! One in two people in Canada are eligible to donate blood, but only one in 81 actually do. [Canadian Blood Services](https://www.blood.ca/) is responsible for the safety of the national blood supply system (along with [Héma-Québec](https://www.hema-quebec.qc.ca/) in Québec) and Canada has one of the safest blood systems in the world! If you'd like to be a blood donor, visit [blood.ca](https://www.blood.ca/) or [hema-quebec.qc.ca](https://www.hema-quebec.qc.ca/) to join Canada’s Lifeline and book an appointment today. #ItsInYouToGive
BLUES: The [Maple Blues Awards](https://www.mapleblues.ca/) is Canada’s national blues awards program. Its goal is to promote blues music across Canada and to recognize outstanding achievement in the field. The Maple Blues Awards have been presented by the Toronto Blues Society since their inception in 1997.
BOGEY: In golf, a bogey means one stroke over par. In Canada, [Triple Bogey Brewing Company](https://triplebogey.com/) embraces the game’s spirit with golf-inspired drinks. Founded in 2014 by Geoff and Megan Tait, the brewery offers premium lagers and ready-to-drink cocktails like Transfusions, Water Hazard, and Azalea. Their products are available at over 400 golf courses and 1,000 locations across Canada, bringing a taste of golf culture to golf fans nationwide.
BORER: In Canada, the emerald ash borer and bronze birch borer are two well-known tree borers found in our forests. The emerald ash borer is an invasive species that affects ash trees, while the bronze birch borer is native to North America and targets birch trees. Both insects live beneath the bark, where they tunnel through wood and disrupt the flow of water and nutrients, making them important considerations in Canadian forest health and tree management.
BOSUN: A "bosun's chair" is a special seat used by sailors, especially the boatswain (or bosun), to perform work high up on a ship's mast. But did you know that in Canada, bosun chairs aren't just for the high seas? These sturdy seats are also used in various industries, like window washing and construction, where workers need to be safely suspended high above the ground. Whether it's maintaining tall buildings in bustling cities like Toronto or Vancouver, the bosun's chair is a vital tool that ensures safety while getting the job done.
BOWER: The word bower comes from the classic card game Euchre, a longtime favourite in Canada! In Euchre, the "right bower" (jack of the trump suit) and "left bower" (jack of the same colour) are the top two cards. With its simple rules, quick rounds, and team play, Euchre has become a go-to game in homes, cottages, and legion halls across the country. It's a true staple of Canadian card culture!
BRACT: It's the first day of spring! Some Canadian alpine plants show off colourful bracts – specialized leaves that look like petals and help attract pollinators. Bunchberry and mountain avens, found in northern and high-elevation regions, use bracts to brighten the tundra and forest floor, announcing the season’s first blooms.
BRAIN: Canada's neuroscience and mental health researchers are among the most productive and influential in the world. Canada is among the world's five most active countries in neuroscience. Canadian researchers have contributed to major scientific advancements in brain research that have furthered the field both nationally and internationally. [Brain Canada](https://braincanada.ca/) plays an invaluable, critical role in this success.
BREAK: Canadian fitness icons Hal Johnson and Joanne McLeod hosted over 300 episodes of the show [BodyBreak](https://bodybreak.com/) which focused on how exercise can be incorporated into daily life. Every show ended with the tagline "Keep Fit and Have Fun!", encouraging everyone to stay active and have fun doing it!
BREED: Canada is home to several unique dog breeds that reflect its history and climate. The Canadian Inuit Dog, also known as qimmiq, is the official animal of Nunavut and has long been used for sledding across Arctic terrain. The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, a clever and energetic hunter, was developed in the Maritimes to lure and retrieve waterfowl. The Newfoundland, strong and skilled in swimming, helped fishermen in coastal waters, while the Labrador Retriever, originally from Newfoundland, was bred to assist fishermen by retrieving nets and fish. These Canadian breeds showcase skill, resilience, and a special bond with people across the country.
BRIDE: War Bride was the name given to the estimated 48,000 young women who met and married Canadian servicemen and came to Canada during the Second World War. These war brides were mostly from Britain, but a few thousand were also from other areas of Europe. Read more about "war brides" on [The Canadian Encyclopedia](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/war-brides).
BRINE: Brine isn’t just salty water – it’s the starting point for one of Canada’s biggest salt success stories. At its Goderich operation on Lake Huron, [Sifto Canada](https://siftocanada.com/) operates the world’s largest rock salt mine, producing millions of tonnes of bulk salt each year. A separate nearby facility pumps up underground brine, then evaporates and refines it into around 95,000 tonnes high-purity, food-grade salt each year. From seasoning kitchens to preserving food across the country, Canadian brine plays a quietly essential role at the table.
BRONC: The [Saddle Bronc](https://www.calgarystampede.com/stampede/rodeo/saddle-bronc) event at the Calgary Stampede showcases the skill and courage of riders as they strive to stay mounted on a bucking bronc for eight seconds, using only one hand. The rider moves his feet from the horse’s neck toward the back of the saddle, in time with the bronc’s bucking action. The cowboy holds on to a braided rein that is connected to the horse’s halter, using it to help balance himself. Riders are judged not only on their ability to stay on the horse but also on their style and control, making it a true test of horsemanship and athleticism. The Saddle Bronc event is a favourite among spectators and highlights the rich rodeo heritage of Canada.
BRONCO: At the [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/), some of the most iconic rodeo action comes from saddle bronc riding, where competitors aim to stay mounted on a bucking horse for eight seconds while matching its movement with control and balance. The challenge, known as bronco riding, grew out of everyday ranch work on the prairies and has become one of the most traditional and technical events at the world’s largest outdoor rodeo.
BUOYS: Buoys are floating markers used to guide navigation and monitor ocean conditions. In Canada, buoy systems play an important role in tracking weather, waves, and marine safety across the country’s vast coastlines. Scientific buoys deployed by organizations like Fisheries and Oceans Canada help collect real-time ocean data used for forecasting, research, and environmental monitoring.
BURBS: "Run the Burbs" is a Canadian television show that brings a fresh and funny perspective to suburban life in Canada. Created by and starring Andrew Phung, best known for his role on "Kim's Convenience," the show premiered on CBC in January 2022. Set in a fictional Canadian suburb, "Run the Burbs" follows the Pham family as they navigate the ups and downs of suburban living with humour and heart. The show is celebrated for its diverse cast and authentic representation of modern Canadian family life, making it a beloved addition to Canada's television landscape.
BURNT: Dr. Wilder Graves Penfield was one of Canada's foremost neurosurgeons. He had a desire to understand the cause of brain illnesses, and made groundbreaking advances in the treatment of seizure disorders. Penfield established the Montreal Neurological institute (the Neuro) in 1934, and along with his colleagues, developed the Montreal procedure for patients with severe epilepsy. The first patient to undergo the Montreal procedure reported smelling burnt toast, and this helped doctors to identify and destroy the nerve cells causing the seizures. Penfield’s experiments with stimulating different parts of the brain helped us learn to map its different sensory areas. Check out this [Heritage Minutes video about Dr. Wilder Penfield](https://www.historicacanada.ca/content/heritage-minutes/wilder-penfield) to learn more!
CACTI: Four species of cacti are native to Canada: pincushion cactus, little prickly pear cactus, common plains prickly pear cactus, and eastern prickly pear cactus. All of these species are at the northern limits of their distribution. In 1985, the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada officially designated the cactus as an endangered plant.
CAIRN: Cairns are stone landmarks that are used as a point of reference for navigation and as a marker for travel routes. In Canada, these rock piles are often called "inukshuks" as many try to replicate the Inuit (and other Arctic peoples') cairns shaped like people and commonly known by that name. A red inukshuk (also spelled inuksuk, plural inuksuit) is found on the flag of Nunavut. In Inuktitut, the term inuksuk means "to act in the capacity of a human." It is an extension of the word inuk meaning "a human being".
CALVE: When glaciers calve, large chunks of ancient ice break away and crash into cold waters, shaping Canada’s Arctic and mountain landscapes. The Columbia Icefield on the Alberta–British Columbia border feeds major river systems, while northern glaciers in places like Baffin Island and Ellesmere Island calve into Arctic waters, helping form icebergs that can drift toward Atlantic waters each spring. Today, increased calving is also seen as a visible sign of a warming climate in Canada.
CANDY: Did you know that [Ganong](https://ganong.com/) candy company in St. Stephen, New Brunswick is Canada's oldest chocolate and candy company? Canada is also home to some unique sweet candy treats, like Smarties, Coffee Crisp, Caramilk, Aero, Crunchie, and Mackintosh's Toffee to name a few!
CANOLA: Developed in Canada in the 1970s, canola is a heart-healthy oilseed crop prized around the world. From cooking oil to margarine, Canadian farmers produce millions of tonnes each year, making it one of the country’s top agricultural exports. Canola is a portmanteau of CANada and OLA (meaning low acid oil).
CANON: In literature, a canon is a collection of works considered especially important or enduring, and Canada has many that stand out. From beloved classics like Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables to influential contemporary novels such as Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale, the Canadian literary canon also includes powerful works by Indigenous authors whose stories reflect the depth and diversity of this land. Together, these books remain cornerstones of Canadian storytelling.
CAPON: A capon is a specially raised rooster known for its tender, flavourful meat – once a staple on traditional farms across Canada. In French Canadian cuisine, roast capon is a cherished dish, often served at Réveillon feasts and other festive gatherings. Its rich, juicy flavour makes it a popular alternative to turkey for festive meals in Canada’s rural and francophone communities and beyond!
CARAT: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! Canadian mines produced 18.6 million carats of rough diamonds valued at $2.25 billion in 2019, making Canada the world's third largest producer of rough diamonds by value.
CARVE: With its many carved pumpkins, sculptures and special effects, [Pumpkins After Dark](https://pumpkinsafterdark.com/) brings magic across Canada. Pumpkins After Dark is Canada’s award-winning outdoor Halloween event, with locations in Burnaby, Calgary, Edmonton, Milton and Ottawa. Featuring over 10,000+ hand-carved pumpkins, this one-of-a-kind walk-through experience is the must-see event of the spooky season.
CAUSE: Happy National Philanthropy Day! Every year on November 15, this day pays tribute to the extraordinary contribution that those involved in the philanthropic process have made to our communities. In 2012, Canada became the first - and remains the only - country in the world to recognize this day. Philanthropy is the spirit of giving without expectation of reward. Canadians continue to be inspired by the dedication of volunteers who devote themselves to improving the lives of others. Philanthropy helps build strong communities and active civic participation by bringing people together to serve a common goal and support a cause. Join us in recognizing the extraordinary generosity and dedication of donors, volunteers and charities.
CENTRE: Perched at the heart of Ottawa, Centre Block on Parliament Hill is currently under an extensive renovation, with a targeted re-opening in the early 2030s. This iconic building, home to the Peace Tower and the chambers of the House of Commons and Senate, has long stood as the symbolic and functional centre of Canada’s federal government.
CENTS: Street Cents is a newsmagazine TV series directed at teenagers that originally aired on CBC Television between 1989 and 2006. Street Cents focused on consumer and media awareness for young people. The show has won several Gemini Awards and even an International Emmy for Best Youth Programming or Series, and was lauded by critics for its efforts to be inclusive and representative of Canada's youth. Jonathan Torrens was one of the original hosts of the show. Street Cents returned in a new format in 2022, led by a group of dynamic content creators. Targeted to teens, the new version of the beloved youth brand has [launched on TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@streetcents) with a focus on making financial literacy useful, relatable and entertaining through daily short form video content.
CHAAT: Happy Diwali! Chaat, the tangy and spicy South Asian street snack, is a favourite during the Festival of Lights. Across Canada, Diwali celebrations feature chaat bursting with flavours like tamarind, yogurt, chutneys, and crispy sev, bringing bold flavours to the colourful festivities. It’s a delicious way to savour the joy and spirit of Diwali!
CHANT: Today is [National Indigenous Peoples Day](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100013718/1708446948967)! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Chants play a vital role in Indigenous culture in Canada, used in ceremonies, healing, and storytelling for generations. These rhythmic vocalizations help preserve history, connect communities, and honour ancestors. Chants, alongside traditional songs, are a way for Indigenous peoples to maintain their cultural identity and pass knowledge from one generation to the next. They are a powerful form of expression and resilience within Canada’s rich cultural mosaic.
CHASE: For over 5,500 years, Indigenous Peoples of the Plains used a strategic chase to guide bison toward cliffs known as buffalo jumps. At [Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump](https://headsmashedin.ca) in Alberta, hunters built stone cairns to funnel herds toward a steep drop. Now a UNESCO World Heritage Site with a museum dedicated to Blackfoot culture, it showcases the skill, planning, and cooperation behind one of history's most effective hunting techniques.
CHEER: In 1606, Samuel de Champlain created the Order of Good Cheer in Port-Royal, Nova Scotia. The Order of Good Cheer was a winter supper club, created to pass the winter months joyously and to combat French settlers from dying of scurvy. Each member of the Order of Good Cheer had to take his turn hunting, fishing, and trading with the Mi’kmaq to create a lavish meal. The night would begin with a ceremonial procession to the table with members carrying the dishes to the feast. The feast leader would lead the procession and he would have the honour of wearing the chain of the Order and a large napkin over his shoulder. To create a lively and fun atmosphere, the dinners would be filled with lots of story-telling, singing and music. Cheers! We hope your day is full of Christmas cheer!
CHESS: Medicine Hat, Alberta is home to the [world's largest chess board](https://mhchess.com/giant-chess-set)! The chess set measures 5.89 metres on each side and the king pieces stand almost 4 feet tall. The board was entered in the record books in 2009, four years after its completion by the Medicine Hat Chess Club. You can find the chess set in a courtyard outside the Medicine Hat Public Library in the summer months.
CHORD: Canada has a long tradition of bringing musicians together, and [Four Chords & The Truth](https://fourchordsandthetruth.com/) is one of the country’s most beloved showcases for songwriters. Launched in Toronto in 2015, this unique event invites artists to share their music “in the semi-round,” taking turns performing songs and telling the stories behind them. The result is an intimate night where every chord struck carries a bit of truth – a perfect harmony of Canadian creativity and storytelling.
CIDER: In Canada, the history of cider could be traced back to explorers like Captain Cook and the Hudson's Bay Company. Cider was used to help prevent scurvy! It may have been the British that first brought cider to Canada, but production flourished in Quebec.
CIGAR: Wordle launched its global word-game craze with CIGAR as its very first answer, a spark that eventually inspired Canuckle’s own Canadian twist. That origin story has a fun modern echo thanks to [Dominion Cigar](https://www.dominioncigar.com/), a Canadian owned and operated company, which released "[The Canuckle](https://www.dominioncigar.com/canuckle/)" cigar this past summer. A perfectly Canadian coincidence linking our puzzle beginnings with a homegrown maker. On New Year’s Eve, it’s a playful way to honour endings, new beginnings, and the words that tie them together.
CLAIM: Today is [National Indigenous Peoples Day](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100013718/1708446948967)! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Gertrude Guerin was a fierce protector of Indigenous people and culture. Living near Vancouver, Guerin spent her adult life helping the Indigenous Peoples of the city. From founding Indigenous organizations, to serving as chief of her First Nation, to helping launch a landmark land claims case, Gertrude had a huge impact on the Lower Mainland area and Canada. The Supreme Court decision in the Guerin case is one of the most important legal judgments in the history of Indigenous law in Canada.
CLANS: Many Indigenous communities across Canada are organized into clans, which play an important role in identity, governance, and kinship. Ribbon skirts often honour these connections, with colours and patterns reflecting clan affiliations, personal stories, or ancestral ties. On January 4th, as we celebrate National Ribbon Skirt Day, we recognize the strength and unity of Indigenous clans, which continue to inspire the designs and meanings behind these beautiful garments.
CLEFT: Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children has played a major role in advancing cleft lip and palate surgery. Beginning more than 50 years ago, surgeons including Drs. W. K. Lindsay and Hugh G. Thomson developed and refined techniques for repairing cleft lips at SickKids. Today, its comprehensive [Cleft Lip and Palate Program](https://www.sickkids.ca/en/care-services/clinics/cleft-palate-clinic/) continues to provide specialized care from infancy through young adulthood, while training surgeons and contributing to cleft care around the world.
CLOUD: Cloudberries are a member of the Rosaceae family and are a relative of the raspberry. These amber berries are a rare find as they are native to cool temperate regions, alpine and Arctic tundra and boreal forest. Cloudberries are also known as bakeapples or bake-apple berries in Atlantic Canada. This herbaceous perennial produces amber-colored edible fruit similar to the blackberry.
COURT: The Supreme Court of Canada is the highest court in the judicial system of Canada. It comprises nine justices, whose decisions are the ultimate application of Canadian law.
COYPU: The coypu, known in Canada as the nutria, is a large, semi-aquatic rodent originally from South America that was introduced here for the fur trade. While it might look a bit like a beaver or muskrat, it has a distinctive long, round, sparsely-haired tail. Coypu were once raised on fur farms in provinces like British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario, making them an interesting, if little-known, part of Canada’s fur-trading history.
CRABS: Canada is the largest producer of snow crab in the world, accounting for about two-thirds of the global supply! The provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec provide Canada and the world with hundreds of tonnes of snow crab each year. Snow crabs have white flesh with a tinge of pink and a slightly salty flavour offering the perfect balance of sweet and briny.
CRAFT: In the past decade, Canada has seen a rapidly growing number of craft breweries popping up. Craft breweries have become so popular in Canada that a new association, Canadian Craft Brewers Association, was formed in May 2019. Sales of craft beer increased tenfold from 2008 to 2018, and it now accounts for 6% of the Canadian market. December 10th is National Lager Day! Lagers are some of the most popular beer styles in the world and Canada is no exception. Celebrate with a craft lager from your favourite Canadian brewery!
CRANE: The Whooping Crane is the tallest bird in North America and the rarest crane species. They stand nearly five-feet tall and are easily recognizable with their snowy white plumage and crimson cap. The only self-sustaining wild population of whooping cranes breeds in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, which straddles the Northwest Territories and Alberta border.
CRAVE: [Crave](https://www.crave.ca/) is a popular Canadian streaming service offering a wide range of content and programming. Launched by Bell Media in 2014, Crave provides Canadians with access to a rich library of movies, TV shows, and original content. It has become a go-to platform for Canadian viewers craving top-quality entertainment, including hit series like "Game of Thrones," "The Handmaid's Tale," and Canadian originals like "Letterkenny." With its extensive selection and exclusive offerings, Crave has cemented itself as a key player in the Canadian streaming landscape.
CREEL: A creel is a traditional woven basket once used by anglers to carry fish, keeping the catch fresh while navigating rivers and lakes. In Canada, creels were common from the trout streams of Ontario to the salmon rivers of British Columbia, often made from willow or split ash with careful craftsmanship. While no longer widely used, they’re still cherished today by fly fishers, heritage enthusiasts, and museums as a nod to Canada’s classic fishing traditions.
CREPE: [Cora restaurants](https://www.chezcora.com/) have been a breakfast favourite in Canada since 1987, when Cora Mussely Tsouflidou transformed a small snack bar in Montreal into a breakfast haven. She crafted a menu filled with fresh fruit, omelettes, French toast, and, of course, delicious crêpes! Today, Cora serves a staggering 60,000 crêpes every week across its many locations, making it a leader in Canada’s breakfast industry. With over 10 million guests served each year, Cora continues to brighten mornings with its signature crêpe creations, like the famous April 89 Crêpe, packed with fresh fruit and custard. Whether you prefer sweet or savoury, there's always a crêpe to flip over at Cora!
CRIED: [The Girl Who Cried Pearls](https://www.nfb.ca/film/the-girl-who-cried-pearls/) made history in 2026 by winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film. Produced by the National Film Board of Canada, the stop-motion film was created by Montréal-based directors Chris Lavis and Maciek Szczerbowski, and is set in early 20th-century Montréal. Featuring Canadian voice actor Colm Feore, it’s a powerful example of homegrown storytelling earning global recognition.
CROOK: A shepherd’s crook is the curved staff traditionally used to guide and protect sheep. Sheep farming has long been part of Canada’s agricultural story, from the rolling hills of the Maritimes to ranches across the Prairies, helping provide wool, milk, and meat for communities across the country!
CROONER: Canadian singer [Michael Bublé](https://michaelbuble.com) is one of today’s most beloved crooners, especially during the holiday season. Known for his smooth voice and charming style, Bublé has become a household name in Canada and beyond. His 2011 Christmas album has become a festive favourite, with classic carols that bring cheer to homes across the country. From fireside gatherings to holiday parties, Bublé’s warm voice has earned him the nickname Canada’s “King of Christmas,” with fans tuning in every December to hear him croon their favourite holiday tunes.
CROWN: As of 2019, there were 47 Crown corporations in Canada, including CBC, Canada Post, VIA Rail, the Royal Canadian Mint, and the Bank of Canada.
CRUDE: Canada has the 3rd largest oil reserves in the world and is the 4th largest oil producer and exporter.
CURLING: Canada’s legacy in curling is unmatched – since the sport returned to the Olympics in 1998, Canadians have consistently stood on the podium. From Sandra Schmirler’s gold in Nagano 1998 to back‑to‑back world titles for Team Homan, Canadian curlers have set the standard on the world stage. At the 2026 Winter Games in Milano‑Cortina, Canada’s men’s, women’s, and mixed doubles teams will once again aim for Olympic gold, sweeping, strategy‑calling, and delivering stones with the precision that has defined Canadian curling for generations.
CURSE: The Oak Island mystery is a series of stories and legends concerning buried treasure and unexplained objects found on or near Oak Island in Nova Scotia. Since the 18th century, attempts have been made to find treasure and artifacts. Hypotheses about artifacts present on the island range from pirate treasure to Shakespearean manuscripts to the Holy Grail or the Ark of the Covenant. A "curse" on the treasure is said to have originated more than a century ago and states that seven men will die in the search for the treasure before it is found. This intriguing tale has been the subject of the popular TV series "The Curse of Oak Island," which follows brothers Rick and Marty Lagina as they explore the island's mysteries.
DAIRY: The Dairy Farmers of Canada logo guarantees a product is made with 100% Canadian milk and milk ingredients, and is free of antibiotics.
DAISY: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! The daisy is a symbol of love, purity, and new beginnings – just like the care and strength of a mother. In Canada, the daisy is known for its simple beauty, blooming across meadows and fields from coast to coast. Whether you're gifting flowers or simply enjoying a peaceful moment in nature, today's the perfect day to appreciate all the moms in your life!
DANCE: Canada is a country rich in multicultural heritage and culture, part of which is dance. Long before we called this land Canada, Aboriginal dancers were practising dance. Powwow dances are beautiful expressions of Indigenous spirituality, history and culture. When more people began immigrating to Canada in the 1900s, they brought with them bits of rich heritage and culture from all over the globe. This influx of international talent is what led to the creation of most of our dance institutions today, including the National Ballet of Canada and the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, Canada's oldest ballet company and the longest continuously operating ballet company in North America. Sikh-Canadian Gurdeep Pandher of the Yukon, has been spreading joy, hope and positivity across Canada with his Bhangra dancing - a traditional folk dance of Punjab. Check out [www.gurdeep.ca](https://gurdeep.ca/) and get ready to dance!
DECOY: Hunters in Canada have been using decoys for generations to attract waterfowl like ducks and geese during hunting season. Decoy carving is even considered an art form, particularly in communities along the East Coast, where handmade decoys were once essential for a successful hunt. Decoys play a symbolic role in connecting Canadians with their heritage and the outdoors, a reflection of the country's strong ties to nature and conservation.
DEEDS: November 13th is [World Kindness Day](https://www.randomactsofkindness.org/world-kindness-day)! The purpose of World Kindness Day is to highlight and encourage good deeds in your community. In Canada, the Chevrolet Good Deeds Cup seeks to inspire young Canadians to do good by transforming the positive values learned through hockey into Good Deeds within their communities. The program has made an incredible impact in communities coast to coast to coast amounting more than 1,000 Good Deeds and over $600,000 to charities.
DELTA: Happy World Rivers Day! Deltas are wetlands that form as rivers empty their water and sediment into another body of water, such as an ocean, lake, or another river. Among the largest deltas in Canada are those of the Mackenzie and Saskatchewan rivers, as well as the Peace-Athabasca Delta. The Mackenzie Delta in Northwest Territories is one of the world's largest river deltas.
DEPOT: In early Canadian history, a depot was more than just a storage spot – it was a lifeline. Trading depots were key hubs during the fur trade era, where Indigenous peoples, voyageurs, and European traders exchanged goods like furs, tools, and textiles. Major depots, such as those run by the Hudson’s Bay Company and North West Company, helped shape trade routes and settlements across Canada. These depots laid the groundwork for many towns and cities we know today!
DINER: [The Chickenburger](https://chickenburger.com/) in Bedford, Nova Scotia, has been part of Canada’s diner history since 1940 and is reputed to be the country’s oldest drive-in restaurant. Known for its chickenburgers, cheeseburgers and shakes, it preserves the look and feel of a classic 1950s diner, complete with a working jukebox. More than 86 years after opening, the landmark remains a throwback to the golden age of diner culture.
DIODE: Canada helped pioneer the next generation of the light-emitting diode. Researchers at the [National Research Council of Canada](https://nrc.canada.ca/en/research-development/research-collaboration/photonics) contributed to early organic light-emitting diode (OLED) technology and continue to advance photonics and thin-film electronics. Today, OLEDs produce the bright, high-contrast displays found in smartphones, televisions and other digital devices.
DIVER: Canada has produced some talented divers over the years who have had incredible success on the world stage. Jennifer Abel from Montreal, Quebec has two Olympic medals for Canada, and her ten medals (six silver, four bronze) are a record for most medals by a Canadian in diving at the world championships. Montreal diver Émilie Heymans was the first Canadian to win medals in four consecutive Olympics. Alexandre Despatie, also from Montreal, is the most decorated male diver in Canadian history, winning two Olympic silver medals and reaching eight podiums at the world championships, including three gold medals. The [2023 World Aquatics Championships](https://www.worldaquatics.com/competitions/1/world-aquatics-championships-fukuoka-2023) are currently taking place in Fukuoka, Japan, featuring Canadian springboard, platform and high divers.
DONER: The doner kebab, a Turkish dish of spiced meat cooked on a rotating spit, inspired a Canadian classic - the Halifax donair! Adapted in Nova Scotia in the 1970s, it swaps lamb for seasoned ground beef and yogurt sauce for a sweet garlic sauce. Served on warm pita with diced onions and tomatoes, the donair quickly became a Maritime favourite and a late-night legend. The donair became so iconic it was named Halifax’s official food in 2015.
DONUT: Canada has the most donut shops and consumes the most donuts per capita of any other country in the world - around 1 billion annually! The donut-eating capital of Canada is Lloydminster, Alberta/Saskatchewan. National Donut Day was last Friday, June 3rd - we hope you celebrated with your favourite donut! In Canada, the preferred spelling is “doughnut”, but most dictionaries list “donut” as an acceptable variant. We wanted to include it in the game since the doughnut/donut is considered by some as Canada's unofficial national sugary snack! 🍩🍁
DOZEN: Did you know egg cartons were invented by a Canadian? Egg cartons were invented in 1911 in British Columbia by Joseph Coyle after overhearing a dispute over broken eggs between a local farmer and hotel owner. Coyle was a newspaper man and part-time inventor. He designed the very first egg carton from newspaper, with cushioned slots for each egg. The next time your dozen eggs get home safely, make sure to thank Joseph Coyle!
DRAWN: In Canada, traditional horse-drawn carioles were a common winter sight in the 19th and early 20th centuries. These elegant, narrow sleds, pulled by a single horse, carried families and goods across snowy landscapes, especially in Quebec and Ontario. Today, carioles are celebrated as a charming symbol of Canadian winter heritage and horse-drawn history.
DREAM: In many Indigenous cultures across Canada, dreams are seen as powerful sources of guidance and healing. The dreamcatcher, which originated with the Anishinaabe people, is a handmade web traditionally hung above a bed to catch bad dreams while allowing good ones to pass through. Crafted from natural materials like willow and sinew, each part holds deep meaning – symbolizing protection, connection, and the cycle of life. Today, dreamcatchers remain a meaningful symbol of Indigenous identity and the enduring strength of traditions across the land.
DRIED: Pemmican is a nutrient-rich food made from dried meat, tallow, and sometimes dried berries. Traditionally prepared by Indigenous Peoples in parts of North America, it has long been valued for its long shelf life and high energy content, making it an essential food for survival, particularly during long journeys across Canada's vast landscapes. Pemmican can be eaten raw or used in prepared meals, and it remains part of Indigenous cuisine today. The word pemmican comes from the Cree word 'pimikan,' meaning 'manufactured grease.'
DRIFT: Along Canada’s coastlines, driftwood is carried by waves, tides, and currents before washing ashore in ever-changing shapes. It has long been used in coastal Indigenous communities for practical purposes such as carving, building, and fuel, and continues to hold cultural and creative significance. Today, it is also widely used in Canadian driftwood art, where artists transform weathered pieces into sculptures, furniture, and natural décor that reflect the beauty of the shoreline.
DRINK: One of Canada’s most iconic drinks, the Caesar, was invented in Calgary in 1969 by bartender Walter Chell to celebrate the opening of an Italian restaurant at the Calgary Inn. Inspired by spaghetti alle vongole, he mixed vodka, Clamato juice, Worcestershire sauce and hot sauce, and the Caesar was born. Canadians are estimated to drink more than 400 million Caesars each year, making it one of the country’s most popular cocktails.
DRIVE: In Canada’s history, the cattle drive was an essential part of the ranching culture, especially in the western provinces. In the late 1800s, cowboys would drive herds of cattle across vast distances to railheads, where the animals were shipped to markets. These cattle drives, especially in areas like Alberta and Saskatchewan, were grueling yet vital to the growth of Canada’s beef industry. The tradition of cattle driving is still celebrated today in rodeos and ranching festivals, reminding Canadians of the tough, adventurous spirit that shaped the nation’s prairies.
DRONE: On a vast swath of southern Alberta prairie, near the tiny village of Foremost, unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) have unrivalled freedom to roam. The Foremost UAS Test Range offers more than 700 square nautical miles of restricted airspace, making it uniquely positioned to advance Canada’s drone technology development. This gives small and medium-sized firms plenty of space to test new drone technologies. It is one of only two places approved by Transport Canada to conduct beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) testing.
DRUMS: Drumming has always been, and continues to be, an important part of First Nations ceremonies, traditions and cultural practices. Drums are often considered sacred amongst Indigenous peoples, representing the heartbeat of people, animals and Mother Earth herself. Drums range in size from small enough for a child to hold, to large enough to seat several drummers around at a ceremony or powwow.
DRUPE: Across Canada, juicy drupes (better known as stone fruits) are a sweet sign of summer. From peaches and cherries in the orchards of Niagara Peninsula to plums and apricots grown in British Columbia’s fertile valleys, these fruits protect their seeds with a hard “stone” at the centre, offering Canadians both a tasty snack and a glimpse at nature’s clever design.
DRYER: The word dryer is forever tied to Sidney Crosby's rise to hockey greatness. Growing up in Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia, Crosby spent hours shooting pucks in the basement of his childhood home, and the family clothes dryer bore the marks of many slapshots sent its way. This makeshift training ground played a part in shaping Crosby into the NHL legend he became. In fact, the battered dryer was even featured in an exhibit at the [Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame](https://nsshf.com/), a testament to the role it played in his journey. Now, as he leads Team Canada as captain in the 4 Nations Face-Off, Crosby continues to inspire the next generation of hockey stars.
DULSE: Somewhat of an acquired taste, dulse is an edible red seaweed that grows in intertidal zones in the North Atlantic and Northwest Pacific Oceans. Dulse picked off the coast of Grand Manan Island, New Brunswick in Canada's Bay of Fundy is said to be the best in the world, specifically that harvested in Dark Harbour.
DUPLE: Duple time, a musical rhythm built around two beats per measure, is at the heart of many traditional Canadian marches and dances. Its lively pulse can be heard in French-Canadian fiddle tunes, Métis jigging traditions, and Maritime folk music that have brought communities together for generations!
EAGER: Canada’s official national animal since 1975, the [beaver](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/official-symbols-canada.html#a3) is famous for its tireless work ethic and ability to shape Canada’s landscapes. Known for building dams that create important wetland habitats, this busy animal inspired the phrase “eager beaver,” a nickname for someone who is enthusiastic and hardworking. A fitting tribute to one of Canada’s most iconic creatures!
EARLY: Natural Resources Canada has developed a national [Earthquake Early Warning](https://www.earthquakescanada.nrcan.gc.ca/eew-asp/system-en.php) (EEW) system designed to provide early detection and warning in areas of moderate to high earthquake hazard and with concentrations of population and infrastructure. In Canada, this earthquake risk is concentrated in western British Columbia, eastern Ontario, and southern Quebec. The EEW system began operation in BC in the spring of 2024 and will begin in Quebec and Ontario in early 2025.
EASEL: Altona, Manitoba is home to the [world's largest painting on an easel](https://altona.ca/p/big-easel)! Artist and art educator, Cameron Cross, developed the vision of a giant steel easel displaying the likeness of Vincent Van Gogh's 'Sunflowers' painting. This landmark stands 76'6" high and is on a 3-legged steel easel. It is a symbol of international fine art and celebrates Altona’s reputation as the Sunflower Capital of Canada.
EATER: The Smoke Eaters (aka Smokies) have existed as both junior and senior hockey teams in Canada since the 1920s. The senior Smoke Eaters won two Allan Cup championships, 1938 and 1962, and two Ice Hockey World Championships playing for Canada in 1939 and 1961. The senior Smokies were the last independent ice hockey club to represent Canada in international competition before the Canada men's national ice hockey team was established in 1963. The current Trail Smoke Eaters are a junior A ice hockey team from Trail, British Columbia, that are part of the British Columbia Hockey League. Learn more about the Smoke Eaters in [Craig Baird's Canadian History Ehx podcast episode](https://canadaehx.com/2022/01/11/the-trail-smoke-eaters-2/)!
EAVES: In Canada, the term "eavestroughs" is commonly used to refer to the rain gutters attached to the eaves of a roof! While "gutters" is the more common term elsewhere, Canadians prefer "eavestroughs" to describe these important drainage systems that help manage rainfall and protect buildings from water damage. This uniquely Canadian term reflects the country's distinctive linguistic features and regional vocabulary!
EGRET: Egrets are a beautiful sight in Canada, particularly the Great Egret, which can be spotted in southern parts of the country during the warmer months! These elegant birds, known for their striking white plumage and graceful flight, are most commonly found in wetlands, marshes, and along riverbanks. The Great Egret was once a rare visitor in Canada but has been increasingly seen in provinces like Ontario and Quebec, much to the delight of birdwatchers and nature enthusiasts. This species has been identified as a priority for conservation and/or stewardship in one or more Bird Conservation Region Strategies in Canada.
EIDER: The [common eider](https://www.hww.ca/en/wildlife/birds/common-eider.html) is a large sea duck that inhabits Arctic and Subarctic coastal marine habitats. The common eider has a distinctive long wedge-shaped bill and is the largest duck in the northern hemisphere. Common eiders breed on marine coasts from Alaska and Arctic islands along ponds and lagoons near the ocean from Husdon Bay and James Bay and along the East Coast as far south as Maine. This species has been identified as a priority for conservation and/or stewardship in one or more Bird Conservation Region Strategies in Canada.
ELBOW: "Elbows Up" is a phrase that means to protect yourself or fight back, and it recently gained attention as Canada flexed its muscle in the ongoing trade dispute with the United States. Just like in hockey, where players use their elbows to shield themselves or push back against opponents, Canada has been using its economic power and strategic policies to stand firm and defend its interests. Whether it's in the rink or the world of international trade, "elbows up" is all about resilience and standing your ground!
ELECT: Canada is a representative democracy. During an election, all Canadian citizens who are at least 18 years old on election day can vote in their electoral district.
ELEGY: April is National Poetry Month in Canada - a time to celebrate the power of words and the beauty of verse! An elegy is a type of poem that expresses sorrow or reflection, often written in tribute to someone who has passed. One of Canada's most famous elegies is In Flanders Fields, written by Lieutenant-Colonel John McCrae during the First World War. This moving poem, penned in 1915, continues to resonate as a powerful symbol of remembrance and Canadian literary strength.
ELVES: [Santa's Village](https://www.santasvillage.ca/) in Bracebridge, Ontario, isn't just a magical summer home for Santa - it's also home to his hardworking 'elves'! Nestled at the 45th parallel, halfway between the North Pole and the equator, it's the perfect spot for Santa’s summer retreat. Since opening in 1955, this charming theme park has welcomed families from near and far, offering a whimsical experience full of holiday cheer during its seasonal operation. The employees - playfully known as elves - help create a world of enchantment, making Santa's Village one of Ontario's most beloved family destinations.
ENDER: Today is [Curling Day in Canada](https://www.curlingdayincanada.ca/)! A time to celebrate the great sport of curling and share the benefits of participation with friends, family, and neighbours in communities across the nation. In curling, an 8-ender is an end where all eight stones score for one team; a very rare occurrence. Curling Canada recognizes teams who score 8-enders with pins and certificates.
ERUPT: Many Canadians are unaware that western Canada lies along the Pacific "Ring of Fire" and has active volcanoes. In fact, there have been at least 49 volcanic eruptions in British Columbia and the Yukon Territory during the last 10,000 years. The most recent eruption in Canada took place at Lava Fork in northwestern B.C. about 150 years ago. Learn more about Canada's volcanoes on NRCan's [Volcanoes Canada](https://chis.nrcan.gc.ca/volcano-volcan/can-vol-en.php) website.
EVERY: Each year, September 30 marks the [National Day for Truth and Reconciliation](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/national-day-truth-reconciliation.html) in Canada. The day honours the children who never returned home and Survivors of residential schools, as well as their families and communities. Orange Shirt Day is an Indigenous-led grassroots commemorative day intended to raise awareness of the inter-generational impacts of residential schools, and to promote the concept of “Every Child Matters”. Equally, it serves as a healing journey for the Survivors and a commitment by all who wear an orange shirt, that every child matters. Reconciliation happens when we all do our part. Consider donating to the [Orange Shirt Society](https://orangeshirtday.org/) to support their mission and future activities at orangeshirtday.org/support.
EXPAT: Canada is home to a vibrant expat community, with people from around the world making it their home temporarily for work, study, or lifestyle. At the same time, there are over 3 million Canadians living abroad, with popular destinations like the United States, the UK, and Australia. Whether in Canada or overseas, expats play an important role in connecting cultures and expanding global networks.
FAKIE: In freestyle skiing and snowboarding, a fakie is when athletes ride or land a trick backward – a move that adds style and challenge to every jump. At the 2026 Winter Olympics, Canadian skier [Megan Oldham](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/megan-oldham/) captured bronze in women’s slopestyle, landing high-flying tricks with precision and even throwing in fakie landings that wowed the judges and fans alike. She carried that same fearless energy into the big air event, where she launched her way to gold and the top of the Olympic podium.
FETES: Joyeuse Fête nationale! The word fête is borrowed from French, where it means “festival” or “party” – and it’s also recognized in English to describe a lively celebration. In Québec, fêtes reach their peak on June 24 for La Fête nationale du Québec, also known as [Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/celebrate-canada/saint-jean-baptiste-day.html). It’s a province-wide party filled with music, fireworks, parades, and pride in French Canadian culture – a true fête in every sense of the word!
FLATS: LeBreton Flats, known colloquially as The Flats, is one of the largest festival sites in Ottawa and is named after Lieutenant John LeBreton, an officer in the Royal Newfoundland Regiment and one of Nepean Township's first settlers. Located in a picturesque spot by the Canadian War Museum and the Ottawa River just 1.5 kilometres west of Parliament Hill, this wide expanse of land hosts the annual Ottawa Bluesfest and will also be the main site for the [2024 Canada Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/canada-day.html) festivities! Join the celebrations tomorrow at LeBreton Flats Park throughout the day and into the evening for Canada's 157th birthday!
FLIRT: [Flirt Drinks](https://flirtdrinks.com/) is a Canadian company founded in Quebec's Outaouais region by two lifelong friends determined to reduce food waste. Their Flirt sparkling lemonades are made with rescued fruit that might otherwise be discarded, turning a simple idea into a refreshing made-in-Canada success story. Cheers to a Canadian company finding a fresh way to make every piece of fruit count!
FLOOD: [Flooding](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/floods-and-flood-control) stands as Canada's most frequent and expensive natural disaster. In fact, floods account for 40% of weather-related disasters in the country! From spring ice jams in the Red River Valley to coastal storm surges in the Maritimes, flooding can impact communities across the country. Some of Canada's most significant floods include the 2013 Alberta floods, which caused billions in damages, and the 1997 "Flood of the Century" in Manitoba. With climate change increasing extreme weather events, Canada continues to invest in flood prevention to keep communities safe from rising waters.
FLUTE: To generations of Canadians, the opening flute of [Hinterland Who's Who](https://www.hww.ca/) is instantly recognizable. The vignettes also had an immense impact on Canadian culture. The series was produced for the Canadian Wildlife Service by the National Film Board to generate interest in Canada's wildlife through one-minute long segments that could air during commercial breaks.. The first Hinterland Who's Who debuted in 1963 and featured John Cacavas' Flute Poem to open the vignette. Then, the voice of naturalist John Livingston came on to describe the animal in the footage.
FLYER: When it made its debut at the 1953 [Canadian National Exhibition](https://www.theex.com/) in Toronto, The Flyer roller coaster was the highest and fastest in the world at the time. Its tallest point was 19 m or 62 ft, and it could reach speeds up to 104 km or 65 miles per hour. Two four-car trains sped along the ride's 796 m or 2,612 ft long track for a total of 32 riders per train.
FORCE: The Canadian Armed Forces is the unified military of Canada, including sea, land, and air elements referred to as the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army, and Royal Canadian Air Force. June 5th was Canadian Armed Forces Day - a day to honour and recognize members of the Canadian Armed Forces who display unwavering courage, sacrifice, and selflessness every day they wear the uniform.
FORGE: [Hamilton Forge FC](https://forgefc.canpl.ca/) is a Canadian professional soccer club based in Hamilton, Ontario, that competes in the [Canadian Premier League](https://canpl.ca/), the top tier of Canadian soccer. Forge FC joined the CPL in 2019 as one of the league's seven inaugural teams. The team name represents Hamilton's industrious roots and aligns with its nickname "Steeltown."
FORKS: The Forks, located in Winnipeg at the junction of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, has been a meeting place for over 6,000 years. Indigenous peoples traded at The Forks, followed by European fur traders, Scottish settlers, railway pioneers and tens of thousands of immigrants. The Forks was designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1974 due to its status as a cultural landscape. The Canadian Museum for Human Rights is located on Indigenous ancestral lands just adjacent to The Forks.
FOUND: Newfoundland gets its name from the phrase “New Found Land,” used in the 16th century in reference to land explored for England after John Cabot’s 1497 voyage. Long before European arrival, it was home to Indigenous peoples such as the Beothuk, whose history and culture are an important part of the island’s story. Today, Newfoundland is part of the Canadian province of [Newfoundland and Labrador](https://www.newfoundlandlabrador.com/), known for its rugged coastline, rich history, and vibrant culture.
FOYER: The [House of Commons foyer](https://www.ourcommons.ca/heritage/en/parliamentary-buildings/past/house-of-commons-foyer) is the Centre Block's primary meeting place. It has vaulted ceilings, marble floors and dramatic lighting. Many Canadians recognize the foyer from media scrums where journalists ask members of Parliament questions after question period and after debates in the House of Commons. The foyer's lower level contains sculptures that depict themes of art, history and philosophy. In the upper level, the stonework shows the coat of arms of each Canadian province. The foyer also contains framed portraits of Canada's prime ministers, contributing to the foyer's dignified character.
FRILL: [No Frills](https://www.nofrills.ca/) is a Canadian discount supermarket chain that keeps shopping simple and affordable. Founded in East York, Ontario, in 1978 and now with over 300 locations nationwide, it proves you don’t need extra frills to fill your cart with fresh produce and everyday essentials. Today, it remains a favourite for Canadians looking for value without compromise.
FRONT: Front Page Challenge was a Canadian panel game about current events and history. Created by comedy writer/performer John Aylesworth (of the comedy team of Frank Peppiatt and John Aylesworth) and produced and aired by CBC Television, the series ran from 1957 to 1995. Famous guests on the show included Gordie Howe, Pierre Trudeau, Malcolm X, and Rick Hansen. When Front Page Challenge left the air in 1995, it was the longest continually running non-news program in Canadian television history.
FROST: Canadian winters can be freezing cold. Uncovered skin in freezing temperatures can get frostbite. But that doesn't stop Canadians from having outdoor winter festivals! [Frost Regina](https://frostregina.com/) was just held in Regina, Saskatchewan from Feb 3-12, 2023. This unique city-wide event celebrates the cold winter climate through stunning light installations, local music, captivating art, and rich culture. Frost Regina is where winter comes to life!
FUNDY: The Bay of Fundy, located between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, is home to the highest tides in the world – reaching up to 16 metres! This natural wonder fills and empties twice daily, moving over 160 billion tonnes of seawater. It’s also a hotspot for fossil discoveries, coastal hikes, and whale watching. Whether you're exploring Hopewell Rocks or catching a tidal bore, the Bay of Fundy is pure Canadian magic!
FUNGI: Canada's forests are home to a wide variety of fungi, including mushrooms, molds, and lichens, playing important roles in decomposition, nutrient cycling, and ecosystem health. With its vast forests, wetlands, and diverse ecosystems, Canada provides the perfect habitat for fungi to thrive. In fact, Canada is home to over 10,000 species of fungi! A fun tribute to these fascinating organisms can be found in Vilna, Alberta, at Mushroom Park, where you'll find the [World's Largest Mushrooms](https://www.vilna.ca/community-profile/things-to-see-do/world-s-largest-mushroom) – a giant sculpture celebrating the area's rich fungal heritage.
GAMER: Canada has earned a place on the global esports map thanks to some legendary gamers. Kingston’s Sasha “Scarlett” Hostyn became one of the world’s top StarCraft II players, while Vancouver’s Artour “Arteezy” Babaev and Kurtis “Aui_2000” Ling are stars in Dota 2. And in Counter-Strike, Russel “Twistzz” Van Dulken from Toronto is a Major champion and one of the most decorated Canadian players ever. From strategy to sharpshooting, Canadian gamers continue to shine on the world stage.
GAVEL: Did you know that despite what movies and television shows might suggest, the iconic courtroom gavel is largely absent from Canada's justice system and Parliament? Following British tradition, Canadian judges, including those of the Supreme Court of Canada, do not use gavels, and neither does the Speaker of the House of Commons. Instead, order is maintained through voice, procedure, and long-standing tradition rather than a symbolic tap of wood found in many legislatures elsewhere.
GENIE: The Genie Awards were given out annually by the [Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television](https://www.academy.ca/) to recognize the best of Canadian cinema from 1980–2012. The Genie Awards succeeded the Canadian Film Awards (1949-1978), and were merged with the Gemini Awards in 2013 to form the Canadian Screen Awards. The 11th annual Canadian Screen Awards were held at Meridian Hall in Toronto from April 11-14 to honour achievements in Canadian film, television and digital media production. Highlights of the awards ceremony air on CBC and CBC Gem tonight on the final day of Canadian Screen Week 2023!
GENRE: The [Juno Awards](https://junoawards.ca/) celebrate the diversity of Canadian music across multiple genres, from pop and rock to country, hip-hop, jazz, and beyond! Since their inception in 1970, the Junos have evolved to reflect Canada's rich musical landscape, adding new genre categories over the years to spotlight emerging talent. Whether it's indie, electronic, or traditional Indigenous music, the Junos showcase the best of Canada's sound! Tonight, the Junos return to Vancouver, British Columbia, marking the city's fifth time hosting Canada's biggest night in music!
GHOST: BOO! Ghost stories are always much creepier when they hit close to home! From gothic hotels to gruesome battlefields, Canada is home to numerous spooky sites from coast to coast! Some of the most haunted places in Canada include: the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel, the Hockey Hall of Fame and Keg Mansion in Toronto, the Fairmont Château Laurier and Jail Hostel in Ottawa, the Tranquille Sanatorium in Kamloops, the Fairmont Empress Hotel in Victoria, and the Plains of Abraham in Quebec City. Are you brave enough to visit them?
GIANT: The Sibley Peninsula just outside of Thunder Bay, Ontario is home to The Sleeping Giant, a series of cliffs which resemble a giant lying on its back. The formation is part of Sleeping Giant Provincial Park and it was voted number one on a list of The Seven Wonders of Canada, and 2007 competition sponsored by CBC. Another famous Canadian giant was "The Friendly Giant", a children's television program that aired on CBC from 1958-1985 with over 3,000 episodes!
GILET: A gilet is a sleeveless vest designed to provide warmth while keeping arms free for movement. In Canada, this practical layer is a favourite among hikers, cyclists, paddlers, and outdoor enthusiasts who need extra insulation during cool mornings and evenings. Whether exploring a national park or opening the cottage for the season, a gilet is a versatile piece of clothing built for Canada’s changing weather.
GINGER: Did you know ginger beef is a Canadian invention? This crispy, sweet-and-spicy dish was created in the 1970s by Chef George Wong at the Silver Inn Restaurant in Calgary, Alberta. Wong’s recipe quickly won over diners and spread from Alberta to the rest of the country, becoming a staple on Chinese restaurant menus nationwide. Today, ginger beef is a delicious example of how Canadian cuisine blends global influences with local flair.
GLOBE: The Globe and Mail newspaper originated from two competing newspapers, “The Globe” and “The Mail and Empire”.
GLOVE: Baseball may be known as America’s Pastime, but it was a Canadian who invented the baseball glove. Torontonian Arthur "Foxy" Irwin was playing shortstop in 1883 when he broke two fingers trying to make a play on a ball hit to him. Instead of coming out of the game, Irwin found an oversized leather glove and stretched the fingers with padding, creating the first ever fielder's baseball glove. Today marks the [Toronto Blue Jays](https://www.mlb.com/bluejays) home opener for the 2023 MLB season. Let's go Blue Jays!
GOALS: Canadian soccer great Christine Sinclair is the world's all-time leading International goalscorer with 190 goals - the most any player, men's or women's, has ever tallied at the international level. The all-time leading goal scorer and most-capped player of the Canadian national team, Sinclair is also its captain. She announced her retirement from international soccer on Oct 20, 2023. #ThankYouSinc
GOLDEN: Canada’s newest team in the Professional Women’s Hockey League is ready to shine on the West Coast – introducing the [Vancouver Goldeneyes](https://www.thepwhl.com/en/teams/vancouver-goldeneyes)! Their name is inspired by the goldeneye duck, a hardy Pacific Northwest native known for its speed and sharp vision. The Goldeneyes bring a new burst of energy to Canada’s women’s hockey scene, and Vancouver fans can’t wait to cheer on their “golden” crew as they take flight in the PWHL.
GONCH: Happy National Underwear Day! In Canadian slang, gonch is one of several playful words for underwear – right up there with gitch, gotch, and gonchies! Most popular in Western Canada, gonch has become part of our quirky national vocab. Whether you’re folding your gitch or packing spare gonch for a weekend at the cabin, it’s a uniquely Canadian way to talk about your unmentionables!
GOOSE: A subspecies known as “giant” Canada geese are the largest geese in the world.
GORGE: Canada is home to some incredible gorges & canyons. One of the best-known canyons in Ontario is the Niagara Gorge, which starts at the base of Niagara Falls, and it ends 11 km downriver, near the town of Queenston, where the famous falls originated some 14,000 years ago. Other notable gorges/canyons in Canada include: Elora Gorge (Ontario's Grand Canyon!), Eau Claire Gorge (Ontario), Grand Falls Gorge (New Brunswick), Coaticook Gorge (Quebec), Ouimet Canyon (Thunder Bay, Ontario), Maligne Canyon (Alberta), Nahanni Canyons (Northwest Territories), Canyon Sainte-Anne (Quebec City, Quebec), and Horseshoe Canyon (Alberta).
GRACE: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! Grace is often part of Canadian holiday traditions, as many families pause on Christmas Day to say a blessing before a meal. Whether it’s a few words of thanks around the table or a quiet reflection on the year, taking a moment for grace reminds Canadians of the importance of gratitude, togetherness, and the little joys that make the season bright.
GRAIN: The grain sector is a key driver of Canada's economic growth, exporting 26.4 million tonnes of wheat in 2020-21 and over $25 billion in exports sales.
GRANT: The Government of Canada offers funding through grants and contribution (Gs&Cs) programs that help support a variety of jobs, research, training and financial assistance across the country. A grant can provide funding to individuals, nonprofits, community organizations and small businesses to support upcoming projects, programs and initiatives. For many Canadians, the ability to access, stay safe and succeed on the internet is still out of reach. To help close this gap, CIRA is launching its 2024 grants program to support not-for-profits, Indigenous communities, researchers and registered charities across the country that are working to bridge that digital divide. [Learn more about CIRA's Net Good Grants program](https://www.cira.ca/en/grants?utm_source=canuckle)!
GRAPE: In Canada, the two main commercial grape-growing areas are southern Ontario's Niagara Peninsula and the Okanagan and neighbouring Similkameen Valleys in south-central British Columbia.
