In 2022, approximately 33,000 acres were used for the cultivation of grapes in Canada. The main grape vine varieties grown in Canada are Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Riesling. Wineries take about 80% of the annual grape production in Canada.
GRAPH: Alexander Graham Bell’s work on the harmonic telegraph helped lead to his invention of the telephone. While working on telegraph systems designed to send multiple messages over a single wire at different frequencies, he explored whether sound itself could be carried as an electrical signal. Much of this research was carried out in Canada, including at his family home in Brantford, Ontario. These experiments with the telegraph ultimately led him to transmit voice electrically for the first time.
GRAZE: Canada is home to over 800,000 sheep, grazing across pastures in provinces like Ontario, Alberta, and Quebec - together accounting for over 70% of the national flock. These flocks support sustainable farming, help maintain healthy grasslands, and are an important part of Canada’s agricultural heritage. Today, there are about 8,400 sheep farms across the country.
GREAT: Although it is unknown who coined the term “Great White North” in reference to Canada, the nickname has been in use for many decades. “Great” because it’s the second largest country in the world. “White” because of the amount of Arctic frozen tundra and snow within the country. Finally, “North” because not only does Canada take up most of the northern half of North America, it also stretches nearly to the North Pole! Canada is also home to the Great Lakes, the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth, as well as Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories.
GREEN: With an abundance of trees, parks and green spaces across the country, Canada is very green! Canadian cities consistently rank among the most livable in the world. In 2022, 72% of the land area of 1,016 cities and towns across Canada was classed as green. A few other notable green things in Canada: Anne of Green Gables, The Green Party, the green roofs of the Parliament Buildings, & Mike Weir's Masters green jacket! April 7th was Green Shirt Day in Canada - a day to celebrate the gift of life & the impact of organ donors. Learn more about the Logan Boulet Effect at [greenshirtday.ca](https://greenshirtday.ca).
GRILL: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! Every year, on the third Sunday in June, families across the country fire up their grills to honour dads with a feast of barbecued delights. From juicy steaks and burgers to fresh fish and vegetables, the grill becomes the centerpiece of many Canadian Father's Day celebrations. It's a time for family gatherings, backyard fun, and enjoying the great outdoors. Whether it's a classic barbecue or a gourmet grilling experience, Father's Day in Canada is a perfect occasion to fire up the grill and enjoy some quality time with loved ones.
GROWN: From PEI potatoes to Alberta beef, and Saskatchewan wheat to Québec maple syrup, so many delicious things are proudly grown right here in Canada! Our vast and diverse landscape supports everything from fresh berries to sweet corn, producing some of the finest ingredients and products the world has to offer.
GUEST: Twenty-five years ago, nearly 6,600 passengers became unexpected guests in Newfoundland after 38 planes were diverted following the 9/11 attacks. Local residents in Gander and surrounding communities welcomed the “come from aways” into their homes and communities, providing food, shelter, friendship and remarkable Newfoundland hospitality. Their story inspired the hit musical [Come From Away](https://comefromaway.com/).
GUIDE: Girl Guides of Canada started on September 7, 1910, and Canada was among the founding members of the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts (WAGGGS) in 1928. Some well-known former Girl Guides include: Queen Elizabeth II, Margaret Atwood, Celine Dion, Sarah McLachlan, and Dr. Roberta Bondar, who juggled Girl Guide cookies in space!
HAIRY: It’s the end of Movember, and things got a little hairy across Canada this past month! From handlebar to horseshoe, moustaches of every style helped raise awareness and funds for men’s health, supporting research and programs for prostate cancer, testicular cancer, mental health, and suicide prevention. Canuckle co-creators [Mark and Jeff proudly joined the cause](https://ca.movember.com/mospace/15437932) – growing their own Mo’s to spark conversation and support this important movement. Thanks to all the hairy heroes across the country who helped make a difference this Movember!
HARDY: Did you know The Hardy Boys mysteries were first written by a Canadian? Leslie McFarlane of Carleton Place, Ontario, penned the original 21 books in the series between 1927 and 1946 under the pseudonym Franklin W. Dixon. A journalist and storyteller, McFarlane brought brothers Frank and Joe Hardy to life with clever plots and fast-paced adventures – setting the tone for one of the most popular mystery series in North America.
HAUNT: [Halloween Haunt](https://www.canadaswonderland.com/events/haunt) is on right now at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto! Halloween Haunt turns the theme park into a scream park filled with Halloween attractions that offer unforgettable thrills and unspeakable horror. From rides, to scare zones, to monsters, it's Canada's biggest haunted wonderland! So, whether you’re seeking heart-pounding coaster thrills or spine-tingling scares, Canada’s Wonderland Halloween Haunt has it all.
HAWKS: The [Golden Hawks](https://cahf.ca/royal-canadian-air-force-golden-hawks/) were a Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aerobatic flying team established in 1959 to celebrate the 35th anniversary of the RCAF and the "Golden" 50th anniversary of Canadian flight, which began with the AEA Silver Dart in 1909.
HELLO: Happy Victoria Day! 👑 [Hello! Canada](https://www.hellomagazine.com/ca/) magazine is a Canadian entertainment magazine that launched in 2006 by Rogers Media. Published weekly, it covers the latest celebrity and royal news from around the world. Hello! Canada has become a beloved publication among Canadian readers, so much so that it is the top-selling magazine on Canadian newsstands and is a leading entertainment brand online!
HERON: Great blue herons are Canada's most widespread heron and are found from the Maritimes to British Columbia. As the largest heron in North America, the great blue heron stands about one metre tall.
HIKES: National Parks Day is the perfect time to lace up your boots and explore some of Canada’s incredible hikes. Trek the rugged peaks of Banff and Jasper in Alberta, discover the fjords and unique geology of Gros Morne in Newfoundland, wander ancient forests in Fundy National Park, or take in coastal views at Pacific Rim National Park Reserve in British Columbia. Each park offers unforgettable adventures and stunning landscapes – grab your boots and hit the trail!
HILLS: On Vimy Ridge Day, we remember the bravery of Canadian soldiers who fought in one of the most pivotal battles of World War I. The rugged hills of Vimy Ridge posed a massive challenge, as soldiers had to climb and fight through difficult terrain to capture the position from enemy forces. The victory at Vimy in 1917 marked a defining moment in Canadian history, solidifying Canada's reputation on the world stage. Today, the [Vimy Memorial](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/en/remembrance/memorials/vimy) stands proudly on those very hills, honouring the sacrifices of those who fought there.
HIPPO: The [house hippo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TijcoS8qHIE) is the subject of a Canadian television public service announcement (PSA) produced by Concerned Children's Advertisers in 1999. The fake infomercial about the fictional critters was created in order to raise awareness about the importance of media literacy. It was produced in the style of [Hinterland Who's Who](https://www.hww.ca/), the Canadian educational series that ran in the 1960s and 1970s. Two decades later, Ottawa-based not-for-profit [MediaSmarts](https://mediasmarts.ca/) brought back the house hippo in a [new commerical](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5R_tOSRynZU) as part of a media literacy campaign called [Break the Fake](https://mediasmarts.ca/break-fake). Real or not, the house hippo will always be a nostalgic piece of Canadiana.
HOLEY: Happy National Donut Day! Ever wonder why donuts have holes? The ring shape helps them cook evenly – crisp on the outside and fluffy in the middle. One Canadian bakery taking donut perfection to new heights is [Holey Confections](https://holeyconfections.com/), an Ottawa-based company known for its 140-layer, flaky, buttery donuts – a croissant-like hybrid that wowed investors on Dragons’ Den with a $500,000 deal. A deliciously holey Canadian success story!
HOUND: In Sault Ste. Marie, the [Soo Greyhounds](https://chl.ca/ohl-greyhounds/) are a junior hockey powerhouse with deep roots and loyal fans. They’ve won three OHL championships and the 1993 Memorial Cup, and even helped launch Wayne Gretzky’s career – he played his first season of major junior hockey there at just 16. The Greyhounds continue to be a symbol of hockey passion in northern Ontario.
HOUSE: The House of Commons of Canada is a democratically elected body whose members are known as members of Parliament (MPs). It is the lower house of the Parliament of Canada (the Senate is the upper house) and provides a link between Canadians and their Parliament. Many laws in Canada first begin as bills in the House of Commons.
HURON: With the longest shoreline of all of the Great Lakes, Lake Huron is one of the most unique lakes on Earth. It is the second largest of the Great Lakes, and the fourth largest lake in the world by surface area. The Huron Wendat are an Iroquoian-speaking nation in Canada, originally living along the St. Lawrence River and between Lake Huron and Lake Ontario.
HUSKY: The Canadian Inuit Dog, commonly known as the Canadian Husky or Qimmiq, is a working sled dog breed that has been used for centuries by Indigenous peoples in the Arctic. Sled dogs are also used for recreational purposes and racing events, such as the Iditarod Trail and the Yukon Quest. Dog sledding, or "mushing," is a popular and unique way to experience the winter wonderland in Canada. What better way to explore the vast, snow-covered landscape of Canada than with a team of energetic huskies leading the way!
HYDRA: Hydra was a crucial and secure radio communications link in Canada during the Second World War. Part of [Camp X](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/camp-x) (a training school for covert agents and a radio communications centre that operated on the shores of Lake Ontario between Whitby and Oshawa), Hydra sent and received Allied radio (including telegraph) signals from around the world. Hydra was the most sophisticated telecommunications centre of its time and was instrumental in coding/decoding information vital to the allied war effort.
HYENA: Hyena Road is a 2015 Canadian war drama film directed by and starring Paul Gross, focusing on the construction of a dangerous supply route (Route Hyena) in Afghanistan. Built and secured by the Canadian Armed Forces as part of Task Force Kandahar, the road has come to symbolize the teamwork, grit, and resilience soldiers showed deep in Taliban‑contested territory.
INDEX: The S&P/TSX Composite Index has provided investors with a premier indicator of market activity for Canadian equity markets since its launch in 1977. With approximately 95% coverage of the Canadian equities market, it is the primary gauge for Canadian-based, TSX-listed companies.
INDIE: Canada's indie scene is bursting with creativity! From homegrown musicians and filmmakers to independent game developers, Canadians are making waves with original, outside-the-box ideas. Whether it's a soulful song, a thought-provoking documentary, or a beautifully crafted game, Canada's indie creators prove that with passion and persistence, you don't need a blockbuster budget to make a big impact. The Great White North is full of independent spirit!
INFUSE: A grassroots idea with a big impact is gaining momentum in Canada. The “[Nanaimo Infusion](https://engageq.notion.site/infusion-2026),” sparked by Tod Maffin, takes place April 24-26, 2026, and invites visitors, especially U.S. healthcare workers, to experience life on Vancouver Island through a welcoming, community-driven weekend. What began as a creative tourism idea has since grown into a broader healthcare infusion initiative, helping connect skilled professionals with opportunities across Canada while showcasing the country’s quality of life.
INLAY: Inlay artwork is a decorative technique that embeds one material within another to create patterns or designs. Indigenous artists in Canada have long used inlay to add meaning and beauty to their work, incorporating materials like shell, bone, stone, or metal into wood and other surfaces. The technique appears in carvings, tools, ceremonial objects, and jewelry, with patterns that often reflect stories, symbols, and connections to the land.
INLET: The west coast of Canada is one of the major fjord coastlines of the world, hosting about 150 inlets. The remote and rugged coastline of British Columbia is indented with stunning inlets that cut deep into the Coast Mountains of the BC mainland north of Vancouver. Inlets can be found across the country from coast to coast to coast!
INVER: The word inver comes from Scottish Gaelic, meaning “mouth of a river” or “river’s edge.” Many Canadian places with Scottish heritage use inver in their names – like Invermere, British Columbia and Inverness, Nova Scotia – to mark locations where rivers meet lakes or oceans. With over 8,500 rivers in Canada, these invers highlight the country’s strong connection to its waterways and natural landscapes.
JEANS: The all-denim look, affectionately known as the Canadian tuxedo, has become a classic style statement! It all started in 1951 when American singer Bing Crosby was denied entry to a Vancouver hotel for wearing head-to-toe denim. Levi's heard about it and made him a custom denim tuxedo jacket to go with his denim jeans - and the rest is fashion history! Whether you wear your jeans dressed up or dressed down, they'll always have a place in Canadian style lore.
JETON: Jetons are small tokens once used for counting and calculations long before modern calculators existed. Today, examples of jetons are part of the national currency collection at the [Bank of Canada Museum](https://www.bankofcanadamuseum.ca/collection/name/view/10/32/74/jeton), highlighting early tools connected to money and commerce. They remind us that even simple objects played an important role in the history of finance in Canada and beyond.
JUNIOR: This year marks the 50th edition of the [IIHF World Junior Ice Hockey Championships](https://www.iihf.com/en/events/2026/wm20), a tournament where the world’s top under-20 players showcase their skills. Canada has long been a powerhouse, winning 20 gold medals and 35 total medals over the decades, more than any other nation. From thrilling goals to unforgettable victories, the tournament celebrates the talent and pride of Canadian hockey’s next generation.
JUNOS: The Juno Awards celebrate the best in Canadian music! Anne Murray has won the most Junos with 25 wins (52 nominations), followed by Bryan Adams (21 wins, 63 nominations) and Celine Dion (20 wins, 75 nominations).
LABEL: More than ever, Canadians are looking to the label to guide their choices. Amid rising trade tensions and growing national pride, more shoppers are seeking out goods labelled “Made in Canada” and “Product of Canada.” A recent survey found that 84% of Canadians check labels to see where items are made, and 77% say they’ll choose Canadian – even if it costs more. That little label is a symbol of pride, connecting Canadians to the people and places behind every product.
LARGE: With a landmass of almost 10 million square kilometres, Canada is the second-largest country in the world.
LAYER: Nanaimo Bars are a Canadian dessert staple originating in Nanaimo, a city on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. It consists of three layers: a graham wafer crumb and shredded coconut base, a custard-flavoured butter icing filling, and a chocolate ganache topping. The Nanaimo bar was popularized nationwide after being highlighted as a classic Canadian dessert at Expo 86. In 2006, the Nanaimo bar was declared Canada’s favourite confection by a reader’s poll in the National Post.
LEDGE: [Balancing Rock](https://www.novascotia.com/see-do/attractions/balancing-rock/2582) in Nova Scotia is a famous volcanic rock balanced precariously on a ledge above the waves of St. Mary's Bay. Called "Nature's Time Post", the Balancing Rock is a narrow vertical column of basalt, balanced on its tip that appears to defy gravity. It is estimated to weigh over 20 tonnes and stands 9 metres (20 feet) tall. It's the most photographed of Long Island's striking basalt formations.
LICKS: Lick's was a homegrown Canadian burger restaurant that first opened on Queen Street East in Toronto in 1980 and grew to more than 30 locations across Ontario. The chain became known for its signature “Homeburger,” fun atmosphere, and quirky traditions like staff singing pop songs while cooking, helping make Lick’s a memorable part of Ontario’s food scene before most locations closed.
LILAC: Lilacs are a spring flower and you can find these in gardens across Canada, but the small village of Franktown, Ontario, part of the township of Beckwith, is special as it is known as the Lilac Capital of Ontario. This Lanark County township near Ottawa is famous for its country road called Lilac Lane bordered by beautiful, fragrant lilac bushes, and is home to an annual Lilac Festival every May. If you love gardens, add the Franktown Lilac Festival to your travel list.
LINKS: The [Perth Golf Course](https://perthgolf.com/), formally the Links O'Tay Golf & Country Club, located in Perth, Ontario is the oldest golf course in Canada to remain in continous play on the same site. The original three-hole course was designed and put in play in 1890 by Captain A.C. Matheson on a portion of his pasture land located beside the Tay River. Golf quickly gained popularity in the area and the course was soon expanded to 9 holes.
LOBBY: In Canada, the art of lobbying has a long history – dating back to the days when political leaders would meet with key figures in government corridors to sway decisions. Today, lobbying is a crucial part of Canadian politics, with professional lobbyists working to represent everything from environmental causes to business interests. The Centre Block of Parliament Hill, with its grand lobbies, is where many of these important discussions still take place, shaping laws and policies that impact the nation.
LOCAL: According to a new report by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, over nine in ten Canadians (92%) said they love having small businesses in their community, but only 13% do most of their shopping locally. Small businesses are the cornerstones of our communities and foster a strong sense of community. We encourage Canadians to prioritize shopping local not just during the holiday season, but all year long! #ShopLocal
LODGE: A beaver home is called a lodge. Beavers live in wetland habitats along lakes and rivers and are some of the best architects in the wild. Some even call them the original Canadian lumberjacks!
LOESS: Extensive deposits of loess (fine, windblown glacial silt) can be found in parts of western Canada, including sections of the Yukon and interior valleys of British Columbia. This powdery soil was laid down by strong winds at the end of the last Ice Age, as retreating glaciers exposed vast areas of loose sediment. Over time, these deposits helped shape fertile soils in some regions and remain an important feature of Canada’s post-glacial landscape.
LOGIC: Happy Star Trek Day! In the Star Trek universe, Vulcans are an extraterrestrial humanoid species known as logical beings who have removed emotions from their daily lives. The official Star Trek Capital of Canada is Vulcan, Alberta. The town even has a prominent display of a Starship Enterprise statue. Live long and prosper! 🖖
LOTTO: Canada's [Pollard Banknote](https://www.pollardbanknote.com/), headquartered in Winnipeg, plays a major role in the world of lotteries! This Canadian company has been a leader in producing instant lotto tickets for decades, supplying games to lottery corporations around the world. Pollard Banknote is responsible for printing roughly 85 per cent of the scratch-and-win lottery tickets sold in Canada. It's also the second-largest printer of those products in the world! From scratch-off tickets to digital lottery options, Pollard Banknote brings a bit of Canadian creativity and security to lotto experiences far and wide. From coast to coast, chances are, the next scratch ticket you buy has a bit of Canadian innovation behind it.
LOWER: The Province of Lower Canada was a British colony on the lower Saint Lawrence River and the shores of the Gulf of Saint Lawrence (1791-1841). It covered the southern portion of the current Province of Quebec and the Labrador region of the current Province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
LUMEN: [Winterlude](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/winterlude.html) is underway in Ottawa and Gatineau, and this year's festivities feature [Lumen Eira](https://limbicmedia.ca/projects/lumen-eira-night-walk/) - a mesmorizing illumination experience animating Confederation Park. This dazzling display blends light and sound, transforming the park into a winter wonderland after dark. Trees glow and pulse with colours synchronized to custom soundscapes, inspired by nature and imagination. Let the interplay of light, sound, and winter's magic draw you into a world where reality is suspended, and imagination takes centre stage!
LUNAR: Happy Lunar New Year! The Lunar New Year is an event celebrated by millions of people across the world on the first new moon of their calendar. It marks the beginning of the new year based on the lunar calendar or lunisolar calendar. It is one of the largest celebrations for Canada's Chinese population, and it is also celebrated by Canadians from Vietnam, Korea and Southeast Asia, among others.
MAGIC: The [International Brotherhood of Magicians](https://www.magician.org/) (I.B.M.) is an organization for both professional and amateur close-up and stage magicians, with approximately 15,000 members worldwide. It was founded in Winnipeg, Manitoba in 1922, and is now the largest organization of magicians in the world. Winnipeg was also home to one of Canada's most famous magicians, Doug Henning, who had a storied career around the world. He retired in the mid-1980s, selling some of his most famous illusions to another famous magician, David Copperfield.
MANGO: Mangoes may need a tropical climate to grow, but that hasn’t stopped Canadians from developing a taste for them. In 2024, Canada imported nearly $250 million worth of mangoes and guavas, with Mexico supplying more than half of the total. From smoothies and salads to chutneys and desserts, this tropical favourite has found a sweet spot on Canadian tables.
MANIC: Quebec is home to [Manic‑5](https://www.hydroquebec.com/facility-tours/tours-general-public/daniel-johnson-manic-5-cote-nord.html), the world’s largest multiple‑arch‑and‑buttress dam, spanning the Manicouagan River. Since its completion in 1970, it has generated hydroelectric power for Quebec and beyond, making it a cornerstone of the province’s clean energy system. Now known as the Daniel‑Johnson Dam, the steady hum of this engineering marvel is a reminder of the massive, reliable infrastructure that keeps Canada running.
MANOR: [Escape Manor](https://www.escapemanor.com/) is known for its interactive and immersive escape rooms in Ottawa, but on September 10, 2017, they organized the world's largest scavenger hunt consisting of 2,732 people! Participants took part in the scavenger hunt in celebration of Canada's 150th anniversary and attempted to complete as many of the 150 tasks as they could throughout the city of Ottawa. Canada now holds the Guinness World Record for the largest scavenger hunt thanks to Escape Manor!
MINER: Happy National Mining Week! Canada has a rich history of mining, with numerous communities across the country built on the back of the mining industry. One such community is [Estevan, Saskatchewan](https://estevan.ca/), known for its coal mining heritage and the iconic character 'Lignite Louie.' Lignite Louie, a fictional character created by the local mining industry, symbolizes the hardworking spirit and resilience of the miners who toiled underground to extract lignite coal, a type of low-grade coal found in the region. Estevan's coal mines played a vital role in powering Saskatchewan's economy and providing employment opportunities for generations of miners and their families. The next time you hear about a miner in Canada, remember the hardworking men and women who helped build the nation's mining industry and shaped the communities we know today.
MODEL: [Little Canada](https://little-canada.ca/) is an incredible attraction in Toronto that features highly detailed 1:87 scale models of Canadian cities and landmarks! The brainchild of Dutch-Canadian Jean-Louis Brenninkmeijer, this miniature wonderland inspired by his love of model trains showcases the beauty and diversity of Canada in a unique and captivating way. The skilled model makers at Little Canada have meticulously recreated iconic Canadian sites such as Niagara Falls, the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, and the Toronto skyline, down to the smallest detail. Visitors can marvel at the intricate craftsmanship and feel a sense of national pride as they explore these miniaturized versions of beloved Canadian locations. Little Canada offers a magical journey through the country, celebrating its rich heritage and stunning landscapes in a truly extraordinary way.
MOIST: [Moist](https://moistonline.com/) is a Canadian rock band that formed in 1992. They released three studio albums in the 1990s, becoming a staple of Canadian rock music. The band, led by frontman David Usher, became a staple of the Canadian alternative rock scene in the 1990s. Moist has been nominated for ten Juno Awards, winning two, including Best New Group at the 1995 Juno Awards.
MOUNT: Canada is home to some impressive mountain peaks, but Mount Logan tops them all at 5956m high. It is part of the St. Elias Mountains in the Kluane National Park and Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Canada's Yukon Territory is home to 8 of Canada's tallest mountains, including Mount Logan.
MUSIC: The Canadian music industry is the sixth-largest in the world, producing internationally renowned composers, musicians and ensembles. O Canada!
NACHO: Nachos may have originated in Mexico, but they've become a Canadian snack-time staple! Whether you're enjoying them at a hockey game, a summer patio, or a cozy night in, nachos are a go-to choice from coast to coast. Some Canadian twists include smoked salmon nachos on the West Coast, donair nachos in the Maritimes, and even poutine nachos loaded with cheese curds and gravy!
NATION: Canada is gearing up to celebrate its 159th birthday on July 1st, marking over a century and a half as a nation. From coast to coast to coast, Canadians come together as a nation to mark the occasion with music, fireworks, parades, and plenty of summer gatherings with family and friends. The word nation comes from the Latin natio, meaning “birth” or “people,” a fitting origin for a country celebrating its own long story of coming together as one. It’s a day filled with pride, connection, and celebration across the country.
NERVE: Canadian neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield helped pioneer the “Montreal procedure” to treat severe epilepsy while patients remained awake. By stimulating different areas of the brain, he could trace nerve responses and map the brain’s sensory regions. Famously, his first patient reported smelling burnt toast during the procedure, helping doctors pinpoint the source of her seizures. Penfield’s groundbreaking work at the [Montreal Neurological Institute](https://www.mcgill.ca/neuro/) transformed our understanding of how the brain and nervous system work.
NEXUS: The word nexus represents more than just a connection - it's also the name of a trusted traveller program that helps speed up border crossings between Canada and the United States! Designed for low-risk, pre-approved travellers, NEXUS lets members use dedicated lanes and kiosks for faster processing at land, air, and marine ports of entry. With over 80 million crossings each year between the two countries, NEXUS helps keep the world's longest undefended border moving smoothly for frequent travellers.
NOBLE: Today, Canada marks the Coronation of its new monarch, His Majesty King Charles III, beginning a new chapter in our country's history. In recognition of the RCMP's 150th anniversary and the Coronation, the King was officially presented with RCMP Musical Ride horse "Noble". The King has shared a personal connection to the RCMP as their Honorary Commissioner since 2012, and on Friday he was officially appointed Commissioner-in-Chief of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
NORDIC: Nordic climates are defined by long, cold winters – something much of Canada knows well, with average February temperatures below freezing across most of the country. Those conditions have helped shape Canada’s strength in Nordic sports like cross-country skiing, ski jumping, biathlon, and Nordic combined, where athletes train for endurance, precision, and resilience in the cold. With the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milano–Cortina starting on February 6, many of Canada’s Nordic athletes will once again put those winter-hardened skills to the test on the world stage.
NORTH: One of Canada's most famous nicknames is the Great White North.
NURSE: Happy [National Nursing Week](https://www.cna-aiic.ca/en/news-events/national-nursing-week)! Annual celebrations take place in Canada from the Monday to the Sunday of the same week as Florence Nightingale’s birthday on May 12. The week draws attention to nurses, increasing the awareness of the many contributions of nursing to the well-being of Canadians. The first integrated nursing degree program in Canada was started at the University of Toronto in 1942. Today, Canada is one of the few countries in the world requiring a bachelor’s degree for entry to practice as a registered nurse (RN). In 2021, there were 312,382 RNs licensed to practise in Canada. Thank you to all the nurses for everything you do!
OILER: The [Edmonton Oilers](https://www.nhl.com/oilers) are a professional ice hockey team based in Edmonton, Alberta. The Oilers were founded in 1971, and played their first season in 1972 as one of the twelve founding franchises of the major professional World Hockey Association (WHA). They joined the NHL in 1979, and went on to win 5 Stanley Cups (1984, 1985, 1987, 1988, 1990) led by captains Wayne Gretzky and Mark Messier. The Oilers are currently in the 2nd round of the 2023 NHL Playoffs and are looking to bring the Stanley Cup back to Edmonton for the first time in 33 years! #LetsGoOilers
OPTIC: Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light, letting information travel vast distances at incredible speeds. In Canada, optic-based networks expand internet access to rural, remote, and northern communities, connecting them to essential services. As more fibre reaches farther corners of the country, optical technology continues to play a quiet but powerful role in helping Canadians stay connected, no matter where they live.
ORBIT: The Manitoba government launched the Orbit program in 1965, which saw unique fibreglass sphere trashcans placed along the province's highways in an effort to reduce the amount of litter. The program lasted roughly till the 1990s across Manitoba highways.
OTTER: Canada is home to both river otters and sea otters. While river otters can be found in every province and territory, sea otters are mainly found on Canada's west coast. Scientists consider the sea otter to be a keystone species - one that modifies and creates its habitat. When it was gone from Canadian waters, kelp forests declined because urchins and other animals that eat seaweed weren't controlled by the otter preying on them. With the return of the otter, kelp forests are in much better shape. This is important because healthy kelp forests provide habitat to fish and reduce coastal erosion by slowing water currents. Sea otters are also of some importance to West Coast Indigenous Peoples - they are depicted in their art and featured in their stories.
OUTER: The vastness of outer space is now a little more Canadian! As the [Artemis II](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/missions/artemis-ii/mission.asp) crew completes its historic lunar flyby mission, Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen is aboard the Orion spacecraft, travelling over 400,000 kilometres from Earth. Hansen is the first Canadian to journey this far into outer space, taking part in humanity’s first trip around the Moon in over half a century.
OVENS: [Ovens Natural Park](https://www.ovenspark.com/) is a privately owned 180-acre pristine reserve of coastal forest, located on the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, along the scenic Lighthouse Route near Lunenburg. For hundreds of years, people have been drawn to the incredible beauty, diverse geography, fascinating history, and spiritual solace that make The Ovens Natural Park so unique. Every year, thousands of park visitors hike the spectacular trails along the cliffs to view the famous sea caves, or "Ovens" for which the park was named.
OWNER: Happy [Canadian Innovation Week](https://canadianinnovationspace.ca/about/)! Business owners are the backbone of the Canadian economy, with small and medium-sized enterprises making up a whopping 99.8% of all businesses in the country. From local coffee shop owners to cutting-edge tech start-ups, these entrepreneurs drive growth and spark innovation across the nation. With their strong entrepreneurial spirit, Canadian business owners are fuelling progress, creating jobs, and helping communities thrive from coast to coast to coast.
PAPER: Charles Fenerty was a Canadian inventor who invented the wood pulp process for papermaking, which was first adapted into the production of newsprint and later the modern paper we use today. Fenerty was born in Sackville, Nova Scotia and was also a well-known poet of his time, publishing more than 35 (known) poems.
PARRY: In fencing, a parry is a defensive move used to block an opponent’s attack – an essential skill in a sport where speed and precision are everything. In Canada, fencing has been gaining momentum on the world stage, highlighted by [Eleanor Harvey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/eleanor-harvey/)'s historic bronze medal in women’s foil at the Paris 2024 Olympics, marking the country’s first-ever Olympic podium in the sport.
PATIO: Happy Victoria Day! Today is a federal Canadian public holiday celebrated annually on the last Monday preceding May 25 to honour Queen Victoria. The holiday has been observed in Canada since at least 1845, originally on Victoria's natural birthday, May 24. Today also marks the unofficial start to the summer season in Canada, and along with the warmer weather comes patio season! However you celebrate this long weekend, we hope you get to enjoy some beautiful weather on a patio and support local businesses!
PEONY: Peonies are a beloved flower in Canadian gardens, known for their vibrant blooms and resilience to our northern climate. The [Canadian Peony Society](https://peony.ca/), established in 1998, is dedicated to the cultivation and appreciation of these beautiful flowers. Peonies are often seen as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune in many cultures, and their lush blossoms make them a popular choice for Canadian gardens. With over 30 species of peonies found worldwide, they thrive in Canada's diverse climates from coast to coast!
PERCH: In Canada, 16 species of perch fish occur, including the yellow perch, the walleye and the sauger. The Canadian waters of Lake Erie are well known for producing monster jumbo perch.
PETTY: Petty Harbour-Maddox Cove is a picturesque fishing village located on the eastern shore of Newfoundland and Labrador, just south of St. John's. This charming community is known for its colourful row houses, stunning coastal views, and rich maritime history. Petty Harbour is not only a haven for fishermen but also a popular spot for tourists seeking to experience Newfoundland's natural beauty and vibrant culture. The village has been featured in various films and television shows, showcasing its stunning landscapes and traditional fishing practices.
PHONE: In 1876, Scottish-born inventor Alexander Graham Bell patented the first practical telephone, a concept that he conceived in Brantford, Ontario.
PIANO: Canada has a storied piano making past, and was home to more than 100 piano manufacturing companies during the peak era of the industry. Piano building in Canada began in the early 19th century and grew into a major, thriving industry between 1890 and 1925. Many Canadians have become noted pianists. Glenn Gould is a bona fide Canadian icon who became one of the most famous and celebrated classical pianists of the 20th century, while Oscar Peterson has had an equally influential role in jazz piano and is considered one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. Other notable Canadian pianists include Angela Hewitt, Chantal Kreviazuk, Diana Krall, Marc-André Hamelin, Anton Kuerti, Charles Richard-Hamelin, and Jan Lisiecki.
PILOT: One of Canada's most famous pilots, Billy Bishop was a Canadian flying ace of the First World War. He was officially credited with 72 victories, making him the top Canadian and British Empire ace of the war. The Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport was named in his honour. Today would have been Billy Bishop's 129th birthday!
PINCH: Happy St. Patrick's Day from O'Canuckle! According to fun folklore, you get pinched on St. Patrick's Day for not wearing green because green makes you invisible to leprechauns. Leprechauns are mischievous creatures, and according to legend, they like to pinch people. Canada's first St. Patrick's Day parade was held in Montreal in 1824. Ever since, parades and festivals of Irish culture have been held annually on March 17th in cities across Canada.
PINGO: Pingos are impressive ice-cored hills found in the Arctic and Subarctic. "Pingo" is Inuvialuit for small hill. The Mackenzie Delta in the Northwest Territories has the highest concentration of pingos on Earth, approximately 1,350 of them. Pingos can be as big as a football stadium, up to 70 metres tall, with a circumference exceeding half a kilometre.
PINOT: Pinot grapes have found a home in Canada’s wine regions, including British Columbia’s Okanagan Valley and Ontario’s Niagara Peninsula. Varieties like Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris have helped Canadian winemakers showcase the country’s unique climates and growing conditions.
PIPER: Rowdy Roddy Piper was one of Canada’s most iconic professional wrestlers. Born in Saskatchewan, he became a global superstar known for his sharp wit, fearless persona, and unforgettable catchphrases. Piper famously entered the ring wearing his signature kilt, accompanied by bagpipe music, a nod to his Scottish heritage. He was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2005 and remains a legend of sports entertainment.
PLAID: The official tartan for Canada as a whole is known as the Maple leaf tartan.
POINT: Point Pelee is the southernmost point of mainland Canada, and is an important rest stop for migrating birds. [Point Pelee National Park](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/on/pelee) is Canada's second smallest but most ecologically diverse national park, and is home to more than 390 bird species and 70 species of trees, some of which are species at risk.
POLAR: Canada is home to about 16,000 polar bears, which is approximately two-thirds of the world's total estimated population.
POLIO: Happy World Polio Day! Canadian researchers at Toronto’s Connaught Laboratories played a key role in developing the polio vaccine. In the late 1940s, Raymond Parker, Joseph Morgan, and Helen Morton created Medium 199, the world’s first synthetic nutrient formula for growing cells. In 1951, Arthur Franklin used Medium 199 to grow the poliovirus, giving Dr. Jonas Salk the tools to develop the first polio vaccine. Their work helped make safe testing possible and led to polio’s eradication in Canada by the 1970s. By 1994, the World Health Organization declared the Americas polio-free, a milestone made possible by decades of vaccination efforts and Canadian ingenuity.
POLKA: Polka Dot Door was a Canadian children's television series which was produced by the Ontario Education Communications Authority (later known as TVOntario) from 1971 to 1993. One of the most well-known elements of the series was the "Polkaroo", a mythical character whose name combines the words "polka dot" and "kangaroo". In 2010, the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television gave Polka Dot Door a Masterworks award, calling it a "groundbreaking children's educational series" that "changed the nature of children's television programming" and "impacted countless young Canadians and raised the international profile of the Canadian television industry."
POLYP: During Men’s Health Awareness Month, it’s a good time to talk about something that often goes unnoticed – colon polyps. These small growths in the colon are usually harmless, but some can develop into cancer over time if left untreated. Regular screening, such as a colonoscopy, can help detect and remove polyps early, preventing serious illness. Across Canada, men are encouraged to take charge of their health by staying active, eating well, and scheduling recommended screenings – because early detection can save lives.
POUND: Lobster season has officially started in Canada in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Canada currently supplies more than half of the world’s supply of “hard-shelled” Atlantic Lobster, considered one of the world’s premier seafood. A lobster pound is where live lobsters are held until they are harvested and sold, like at [Halls Harbour Lobster Pound](https://hallsharbourlobster.com/) in Nova Scotia and [Lobster on the Wharf](https://www.lobsteronthewharf.com/) in PEI, known as MacKinnon's Lobster Pound to locals.
PRANK: April Fools' Day wouldn't be the same without a classic prank, and one of the most iconic prank devices, the whoopee cushion, was invented in Toronto in the 1930s! Created by the JEM Rubber Company, this cheeky contraption has been a prankster's favourite for nearly 100 years, delivering laughs and a few embarrassed giggles along the way. A simple but brilliant invention, the whoopee cushion proves that a well-placed prank never goes out of style!
PRISM: [Prism](https://prism.ca/) (styled as PRiSM) is a Canadian rock band formed in Vancouver in 1977. Their classic line-up consisted of lead singer Ron Tabak, guitarist Lindsay Mitchell, keyboardist John Hall, bassist Allen Harlow and drummer Rocket Norton. They have released a total of eight studio albums, three compilation albums and one live album and they won the Canadian music industry Juno Award for 'Group of the Year' in 1981. A pre-fame Bryan Adams contributed as a songwriter to several early Prism releases.
PRUNE: Vinarterta is a classic holiday cake that has become more common in Canada than Iceland, where it is believed to have originated. The beautiful celebration cake traditionally consists of multiple uniform layers of biscuits sandwiched together with a homemade prune jam that’s loaded with wintry spices. The recipe was brought to Manitoba by Icelandic immigrants to Canada, many of whom initially settled at New Iceland on the west shore of Lake Winnipeg. Manitoba’s Icelandic population has made the vínarterta a staple dessert in the region. If you want to try some authentic Vinarterta, check out [The Icelandic Festival of Manitoba](https://www.icelandicfestival.com/) "Islendingadagurinn" in Gimli, Manitoba which runs from Aug 4-7, 2023!
PUREE: Pumpkin pie is a beloved dessert for Thanksgiving in Canada, and it often features pumpkin puree as a key ingredient. This smooth, sweet mixture is essential for making delicious pumpkin pie, a favourite dessert on Canadian Thanksgiving tables. In fact, 60% of Canadians indulge in this delightful dessert every Thanksgiving, highlighting its popularity across the country. Whether you're using fresh pumpkins or canned puree, this comforting dessert is sure to bring warmth and joy to Thanksgiving celebrations.
QUIET: The Quiet Revolution ("Révolution tranquille" in French) refers to a significant period of socio-political and socio-cultural transformation in French Canada, particularly in Quebec, following the election of 1960. This vivid yet paradoxical description of the period was first used by an anonymous writer in The Globe and Mail. The Quiet Revolution is a major reference point used by successive Québec governments in power since the Liberal defeat in 1966.
QUINT: The Dionne quintuplets are the first quintuplets known to have survived their infancy. The identical girls were born on May 28, 1934 just outside Callander, Ontario, near the village of Corbeil. The birth and survival of five identical, premature and undersized infants – Yvonne, Annette, Cécile, Émilie, and Marie – was an unprecedented event that attracted international attention. All five survived to adulthood. In 2018, the birth of the quintuplets was named a National Historic Event. Happy 89th Birthday to the Dionne quints!
QUOTA: Fishing quotas play an important role in managing Canada’s marine resources. In 1992, the federal government placed a major moratorium on the Atlantic cod fishery after decades of overfishing led to the collapse of cod stocks, dramatically impacting communities across Newfoundland and Labrador. Since then, strict quotas and management measures have been used to help protect remaining fish populations and support the long-term sustainability of Canada’s fisheries.
RADII: Radii are the lines from the centre to the edge of a circle – the building blocks of Pi, celebrated worldwide on March 14. In Canada, math lovers mark Pi Day with everything from circular pancakes to STEM activities, and Canadian mathematician John Charles Fields, namesake of the prestigious Fields Medal, reminds us that understanding radii is key to the discoveries honoured at the highest levels of mathematics.
RALLY: May 17 marks the [International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia, and Transphobia](https://may17.org/). Canada has a rich history of rallies and protests, where citizens come together to advocate for change and raise awareness about important social and political issues. The 'We Demand' rally, which took place on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario on August 28, 1971, was the first large-scale LGBTQ2+ rally in Canadian history. The rally marked a pivotal moment in Canada's LGBTQ2+ rights movement. Today, rallies and protests remain an important part of Canada's democratic process, providing a platform for citizens to voice their concerns and hold their government accountable.
RAMEN: Did you know that ramen has found a special place in Canada’s diverse culinary landscape? While traditionally a Japanese dish, ramen shops have popped up across Canadian cities, from Vancouver to Toronto, with many chefs adding local twists. The first dedicated ramen shop in Canada opened in Vancouver in 1996, and since then, the dish has been embraced coast to coast. Whether it’s the cold winters that call for a warm, comforting bowl or the multicultural nature of the country, Canadians have welcomed ramen as part of their rich food scene!
RANCH: Cattle ranching is the most common type of ranching in Canada, with over 70% of ranches raising beef cattle. Canada is the fourth-largest beef and cattle exporter in the world, with over 60,000 cattle farms and ranches. There are approximately 3.7 million beef cattle in Canada, of which nearly half are in Alberta.
RANTS: Canadians might be known for being polite, but we do love a good rant! Rick Mercer's iconic "Rick’s Rant" segments hilariously tackled politics and Canadian quirks from back alleys across the country. And who could forget the famous rant from the Molson Canadian commercial back in 2000, where Joe proudly declared "[I AM CANADIAN!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WMxGVfk09lU)" Every good rant tells a story and carries a touch of Canadian pride.
READS: [Canada Reads](https://www.cbc.ca/books/canadareads) is an annual "battle of the books" competition organized and broadcast by Canada's public broadcaster, the CBC. During Canada Reads, five Canadian personalities champion five different books, with each advocate extolling the merits of one of the titles. The Canada Reads 2023 winner was ["Ducks: Two Years in the Oil Sands"](https://www.cbc.ca/books/ducks-by-kate-beaton-1.6559688) by author Kate Beaton, championed by Jeopardy super-champion Mattea Roach.
REBAR: Rebar (short for "reinforcing bar") is a key material in construction, providing strength and durability to concrete structures. Canada has a strong steel industry, with major production hubs in Ontario, Quebec, and Alberta supplying high-quality rebar for bridges, buildings, and infrastructure projects across the country. Many Canadian steel mills, such as those in Hamilton, Ontario (nicknamed "Steeltown") manufacture rebar using recycled steel, making it both strong and sustainable! So whether it's a towering skyscraper or a sturdy hockey arena, Canadian-made rebar helps build the backbone of our nation!
REEFS: Canada is home to rare glass sponge reefs off the coast of British Columbia, some of the only living reefs of their kind in the world. These ancient underwater structures can be thousands of years old and provide vital habitat for marine life, forming complex ecosystems in the deep, cold waters of the Pacific.
REIGN: The reign of Canada's new monarch, King Charles III, began when Queen Elizabeth II died on September 8. Queen Elizabeth II was Canada's monarch for over 70 years, making her the longest reigning monarch in Commonwealth history.
RELIC: Robert Allan Clothier was a Canadian stage and television actor most famous for his role as Relic on the CBC television series, The Beachcombers. He portrayed Bruno Gerussi's rival beachcomber, Relic - a curmudgeonly, conniving man of Welsh descent who lived on a house boat and used his jetboat to outrun and challenge Nick's claims to logs. After landing this memorable role, Clothier became a household face among viewers, as the show originally aired from 1972 to 1990, one of the longest running Canadian television dramas of all time.
RESET: For many Canadians, spring brings more than warmer weather – it’s the season for a full household reset. From washing windows and airing out rooms to clearing garages and tackling winter clutter, spring cleaning has long been a tradition across Canada. After months spent indoors during the colder seasons, many families use this time of year to refresh their homes, routines, and outlook for the months ahead.
RESIN: Canada’s forests are filled with trees that produce resin, a sticky substance that helps conifers like pines, spruces, and firs seal wounds and defend against pests and disease. For generations, Indigenous peoples across Canada have used tree resins and pitches for waterproofing, repairs, and other practical applications. Today, tree resin continues to be used in products like varnishes, adhesives, and other materials, making it a remarkable natural resource found throughout Canada’s wilderness.
REVEL: Each March 17, communities across Canada revel in the spirit of St. Patrick’s Day! From lively parades to seas of green, people across the country join in celebrating Irish heritage. In fact, Canada is home to one of the largest Irish diasporas outside Ireland, with millions of Canadians tracing at least some of their roots to the Emerald Isle.
RIDER: [Canadian equestrian](https://equestrian.ca/) riders have shone brightly on the world stage in both dressage and eventing! [Ian Millar](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/ian-millar/), affectionately known as "Captain Canada," has competed in a record 10 Olympic Games, winning a team silver medal in show jumping at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. In dressage, Canada brought home a bronze medal in team dressage from the 1988 Seoul Olympics. Canada’s equestrian success continues to inspire and showcase the dedication and talent of its riders.
RIDGE: The Battle of Vimy Ridge, during the First World War, is Canada's most celebrated military victory – an often mythologized symbol of the birth of Canadian national pride and awareness.
RIGHT: The [Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/csj-sjc/rfc-dlc/ccrf-ccdl/) protects a number of rights and freedoms, including freedom of expression and the right to equality. It forms part of our Constitution – the highest law in all of Canada – and is one of our country’s greatest accomplishments. Every year on April 17th, we celebrate the anniversary of the Charter which was signed in 1982.
RINGS: Curling is played on a rink or sheet of ice that has 3 concentric rings and the button which make up the house or target. "Roar of the Rings" was the name of the Canadian Olympic Curling Trials, and "[Rocks & Rings](https://rocksandrings.com/)" is a Curling Canada program designed to introduce the sport of curling to children. The [2023 Scotties Tournament of Hearts](https://www.curling.ca/2023scotties/) is currently underway in Kamloops, BC and the members of the winning team receive gold rings in the four-heart design of the Tournament of Hearts logo. The winner will represent Canada at the World Women's Curling Championship!
ROBIN: The return of the robin is a sure sign of Spring in Canada! American Robins begin to arrive at their breeding grounds in southern areas of Canada in March each year. Few birds are as familiar to the Canadian public as the robin. Its plumage is easily recognizable, and it is one of the first birds to sing in the morning and one of the last to be heard at night.
ROBOT: Canada has a thriving robotics industry, and many of the most famous and inventive real-world robots have Canadian origins, many of which have taken to the stars. The iconic Canadarm & Canadarm 2 robotic arms have supported space shuttle missions for decades, and Dextre is a versatile robot that maintains the International Space Station (ISS). Part of Canada's contribution to the Station, it is the most sophisticated space robot ever built.
ROPER: A roper is a person who uses a lasso to catch an animal, especially in a rodeo. The Calgary Stampede features the best riders, racers and ropers each year!
ROUSE: "The Rouse" is a bugle call most often associated with the military in Commonwealth countries. It is commonly played following "Last Post" at military services. "The Rouse" was traditionally played following "Reveille", which was a bugle call played in the morning to wake soldiers up.
ROUTE: Today is the 2023 Terry Fox Run! The event is a classic Canadian tradition every Fall with communities and runners across the country coming together to fundraise for cancer research. It is the world's largest one-day fundraiser for cancer research. Terry Fox's route across Canada for his Marathon of Hope started in St. John's, Newfoundland & Labrador and ended early in Thunder Bay, Ontario, but if you stretch the total distance he ran (5,373 km) into a straight line, his route reaches all the way to Vancouver Island's west coast. You can donate to the [Terry Fox Foundation](https://terryfox.org/) in honour of Terry at [terryfox.org](https://terryfox.org/).
ROWDY: Roderick George Toombs, better known as "Rowdy" Roddy Piper, was a Canadian professional wrestler and actor. Piper was best known to international audiences for his work with the World Wrestling Federation (now WWE) and World Championship Wrestling between 1984 and 2000. Although he was Canadian, Piper was billed as coming from Glasgow and was known for his signature kilt and bagpipe entrance music. In 2005, Piper was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame by Ric Flair, who dubbed him "the most gifted entertainer in the history of professional wrestling".
ROWEL: The [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/) starts today! A rowel is the small, spinning toothed wheel at the end of a cowboy's spur, a familiar sight on Canadian ranches since the open-range cattle era of the 1880s. Every July, thousands of cowboys and cowgirls wearing spurs and chaps gather in Calgary for the Stampede, the world's largest outdoor rodeo, celebrating a western tradition that's become an iconic part of Canada's heritage.
ROWER: A total of 43 Olympic medals (including 10 gold medals) have been won by Canadian rowers, making rowing Canada's third-most successful summer Olympic sport (behind athletics and swimming).
RUGBY: Buoyed by its inclusion in the 2016 Olympic Games, Rugby is one of the fastest growing team sports in Canada, particularly in youth and women.
RUSTY: Rusty was the cheerful puppet rooster on The Friendly Giant, a classic Canadian children’s television show that aired from 1958 to 1985. Voiced and puppeteered by Canadian Rod Coneybeare, Rusty lived in a book bag that hung on the castle wall, delighting generations of viewers and becoming a symbol of warmth, friendship, and fun in households across Canada.
SANDY: While Canada is famous for its mountains and forests, it also has some of the world's most beautiful sandy beaches. One of the gems is [Sandbanks Provincial Park](https://www.ontarioparks.ca/park/sandbanks) in Ontario, which features the largest freshwater sandbar and dune system in the world! Another beach lover's paradise is Cavendish Beach in Prince Edward Island, with its red sand and rolling dunes. Alongside Wasaga Beach in Ontario, the longest freshwater beach in the world, these natural beauties offer picturesque sandy getaways for visitors and Canadians alike.
SANTA: HO HO HO! Did you know that Santa Claus is a legal Canadian citizen? Santa was declared a full Canadian citizen in 2008 by Canada’s Immigration Minister and was even issued a Canadian passport in 2013! Of course, Santa also has the most famous postal code in Canada: H0H 0H0. Santa's closest neighbours are the Canadians living in Alert, Nunavut, only 820 kilometres from the North Pole. Merry Christmas, eh?
SCARY: Halloween is the perfect time for all things scary in Canada! From haunted streets to eerie historic sites, Canadians can’t resist a good fright. Across the country, ghost stories, creepy decorations, and centuries-old landmarks bring chills and thrills to the season. Creepy costumes, scary decorations, and spine-chilling stories make Halloween the perfect time to embrace the supernatural!
SCAUP: The scaup is a type of diving duck found in Canada, known for its sleek black-and-white plumage and love for deep-water foraging. There are two main species of scaup in Canada: the Lesser Scaup and the Greater Scaup. They're also known for their incredible migratory journeys, flying thousands of kilometres between breeding grounds in Canada and wintering spots along the coasts of the United States.
SCREE: Canada's towering mountain ranges, from the Rockies in Alberta to the Saint Elias Mountains in the Yukon, are home to dramatic slopes covered in scree - loose rock fragments that gather at the base of steep cliffs. These rocky patches are common sights on alpine hikes, especially above the treeline where vegetation thins out. While tricky to hike on, scree slopes are vital habitats for mountain wildlife like marmots and pikas, and they offer geologists a glimpse into the natural erosion shaping Canada's rugged terrain!
SCROD: In Canada's Maritime provinces, "scrod" is a term used to describe young, white fish like cod or haddock that are commonly enjoyed as part of the local cuisine. The word "scrod" originally comes from New England, but it's also embraced in the Maritimes, where fresh fish is a staple of the diet. Whether baked, broiled, or fried, scrod is a tasty reminder of the rich fishing heritage that has sustained coastal communities in Atlantic Canada.
SEATS: Today is [Election Day](https://www.elections.ca/)! In Canada's 2025 federal election, the House of Commons expanded to 343 seats, reflecting the country's growing population. This change underscores the dynamic nature of Canada's democracy, ensuring that representation in Parliament keeps pace with demographic shifts. Each seat represents a unique riding, and the party that secures at least 172 seats forms a majority government. This adjustment emphasizes the importance of every vote, as even a single seat can influence the balance of power in Parliament.
SERAC: A serac is a towering pinnacle of glacier ice created as moving ice fractures over steep terrain. Canada is home to spectacular seracs, from the Columbia Icefield in the Rockies to the massive glaciers of Kluane National Park and Reserve in Yukon.
SERGE: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or “Mounties,” are known for their iconic uniforms that feature the iconic scarlet tunic called a red serge.
SERVE: For more than 100 years, millions of Canadians have proudly served our country in uniform. While the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) are known to put their lives on the line to support international operations, they also fulfill important roles on home soil. They provide national and regional security, serve on search and rescue missions and respond to natural disasters. On this Remembrance Day, we honour those who made the ultimate sacrifice. Lest we forget.
SEVEN: The Group of Seven was a group of painters from 1920 to 1933, best known for their paintings inspired by the Canadian landscape that initiated the first major Canadian national art movement.
SEWED: On [National Flag of Canada Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/national-flag-canada-day.html), we remember the woman who literally sewed Canada’s identity into history. In 1964, Ottawa civil servant Joan O’Malley stayed late into the night at her Singer sewing machine to sew the first Canadian flag, turning cloth and thread into a symbol that would unite a nation. Every stitch carried pride, purpose, and the promise of a flag that would fly over homes, schools, and Parliament – and, of course, soar above Canadian athletes at the Olympics!
SEWER: [Flin Flon](https://cityofflinflon.ca/), Manitoba is known for its unique above-ground “sewer boxes,” wooden-covered utility structures built because the rocky Canadian Shield made underground installation difficult. In the city’s early development, they also doubled as pedestrian walkways and remain a distinctive part of the local infrastructure today.
SHAFT: Goderich, Ontario is home to the world's largest salt mine! Located beneath Lake Huron, the mine shaft is as deep as the height of the CN Tower. Operating since 1959, the rock salt produced at the Sifto Salt Mine is used to keep citizens in North America safe as they travel through winter snow and ice.
SHAKE: Did you know Canada has an island that literally shakes? Tremble Island, located in British Columbia’s Seymour Inlet, experiences a phenomenon where the ground quivers due to the power of the water currents surrounding it. This inlet has some of the fastest tidal surges in the world, and at peak tides, the force of the water is so intense that it causes the entire island to tremble! Visitors to Tremble Island are in for a unique (and slightly shaky) experience, showcasing the raw power of Canada’s incredible natural landscapes.
SHAVE: Every Movember,Canadians start the month with a clean shave before growing moustaches to raise awareness for men’s health. The movement began in Australia in 2003 and quickly spread worldwide, with Canada becoming one of the top fundraising countries. Through the power of the mo’, Canadians help support research and programs focused on mental health, prostate cancer, testicular cancer, and suicide prevention. Canuckle co-creators Mark & Jeff are growing their moustaches to support the cause! [Visit our Mo Space and make a donation](https://ca.movember.com/mospace/15437932) for all the dads, brothers, sons, and men in your life.
SHAWL: Powwow dances are beautiful expressions of Indigenous spirituality, history and culture. There are a variety of regional dance styles performed by men, women and children across North America. Women were traditionally required to wear shawls as a sign of proper etiquette when in a dancing arena. The characteristic feature of the women's [Fancy Shawl Dance](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/powwow-dances#WomensFancyShawlDance) - the elaborate shawl - is uniquely decorated by the dancer with distinct ornaments, beadwork and fringes. Though diverse in terms of regalia, footwork and origin stories, powwow dances remain a testament to Indigenous history, heritage and identity.
SHEAF: The sheaf toss is a classic event at the [Antigonish Highland Games](https://antigonishhighlandgames.ca/), which celebrates its 160th edition this year! Established in 1863, it's the oldest continuous Highland Games outside of Scotland. In the sheaf toss, athletes use a pitchfork to launch a burlap bag stuffed with straw over a high bar – showcasing strength, skill, and Scottish tradition. From kilts to cabers, Antigonish brings the Highlands to Nova Scotia every summer!
SHEET: In Canada, curling is more than just a sport - it's a winter tradition! The game is played on a long, narrow stretch of ice called a sheet, where teams slide granite stones toward a target. Canada is home to nearly 1,000 curling clubs and some of the world's best curlers. Today, all eyes are on Kelowna, BC, for the final of the [Montana's Brier](https://www.curling.ca/2025brier/)! The country's top men's teams are battling it out on the sheets for a chance to be crowned Canadian champions. Hurry hard!
SHIRT: Feb 22 is Anti-Bullying Day, also known as [Pink Shirt Day](https://www.pinkshirtday.ca/), where people wear a pink-coloured shirt to stand against bullying. The initiative was started in Canada in 2007 by two Nova Scotia teenagers when a fellow Grade 9 student in Berwick was being teased and bullied for wearing a pink shirt on the first day of school.
SIXTH: June 6th marks the anniversary of D-Day, when Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy during the Second World War in 1944. Known as Operation Overlord, the invasion began on the sixth day of June and became one of the largest amphibious military operations in history. Canadian forces played a major role on Juno Beach, fighting alongside Allied troops in a pivotal moment that helped turn the tide of the war in Europe.
SIXTY: In Canada, the 60th parallel forms the southern mainland boundary of the northern territories of Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut. Accordingly, "North of 60" is an expression often used for the territories. There was even 1990s TV show on CBC called North of 60, a drama depicting life in the sub-Arctic northern boreal forest.
SKINK: The Common Five-lined Skink is one of Canada's native lizard species. Found in Ontario along the southern edge of the Canadian Shield, these small, speedy reptiles prefer warm, rocky habitats and forested areas. Juveniles are especially eye-catching with their bright blue tails, which they can detach to escape predators - a clever survival trick! While their tails eventually regrow, it takes a lot of energy, so they don't drop them unless absolutely necessary. As a cold-blooded species, skinks bask in the sun to stay warm, making them a rare but fascinating sight in the Canadian wild!
SLEDS: “Toboggan” is from the Mi'kmaq word “tobakun,” which means sled. In fact, the Inuit made the first toboggans out of whale bone and used it to transport people and belongings across the snowy tundra. Guy Martin holds the world record for fastest speed on a gravity powered snow sled at over 134 km/h in 2014!
SLEET: Sleet is a familiar part of Canadian winters, forming when snowflakes melt into raindrops and then refreeze before hitting the ground. Canada experiences some of the widest temperature swings on Earth, which makes mixed precipitation like sleet especially common in late fall and early spring. In fact, parts of southern Canada can see all four types of precipitation – rain, snow, sleet, and freezing rain – within the same day!
SLICE: In Newfoundland and Labrador, a humble slice of bologna takes on legendary status! Affectionately known as “Newfie steak,” thick slices of this processed meat are pan-fried until crispy and golden brown. Served solo, in sandwiches, or even at community breakfasts, it’s a beloved comfort food with big flavour and even bigger heart. Whether sizzling in a skillet or served on a bun with mustard, it’s a slice of East Coast tradition!
SLIDE: The Frank Slide was a massive rockslide that buried part of the mining town of Frank in the District of Alberta of the North-West Territories (now the province of Alberta) on April 29, 1903. The site of the disaster, which remains nearly unchanged since the slide, is now a popular tourist destination. It has been designated a provincial historic site of Alberta and is home to an interpretive centre that receives over 100,000 visitors annually. Visit [frankslide.ca](https://frankslide.ca) to learn more about Canada's deadliest rockslide.
SMART: Canada is the most educated country globally, with over 56% of adults meeting the OECD criteria of residents aged 25 to 64 who have completed some form of tertiary education.
SMELT: Fresh smelt are a cold-weather harvest for fishers in Canada. Pan-fried with flour and butter, some rank smelt right up there with lobster and scallops on the tasty-scale. Smelts can be found in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, as well as some freshwater lakes across Canada. Indigenous peoples in Canada native to the Great Lakes regions were both familiar and partially dependent upon smelts as a dietary source of protein and omega fats.
SNACK: June 7 is National Donut Day! Donuts are one of Canada's most beloved snack foods and these sweet treats have become a staple of Canadian culture. In fact, Canada has the most donut shops and consumes the most donuts per capita of any other country in the world - around 1 billion annually! Whether you prefer a classic style donut or a more elaborate creation, donuts hold a special place in the hearts (and stomachs) of Canadians from coast to coast.
SNEER: Remember Cyril Sneer from The Raccoons? That pink-nosed villain with a love for money and a signature scowl was part of a classic Canadian cartoon created by Kevin Gillis and produced by Sheldon Wiseman. Set in the Evergreen Forest, the series followed raccoon friends who often found themselves standing up to Cyril's scheming ways - all while promoting messages of friendship, conservation, and doing the right thing. A true gem of Canadian animation!
SNOWY: On February 10, 1999, Tahtsa Lake, British Columbia got hit with 145 cm (4'9") of snow in ONE day!
SONGS: The [2024 Juno Awards](https://junoawards.ca/) are taking place in Halifax, Nova Scotia tonight to honour achievements in Canadian music in 2023. The ceremony will be hosted by Nelly Furtado. The Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) votes and awards outstanding Canadian artists for their top songs, videos, and albums released throughout the year.
SOOTY: The Sooty Grouse is a large, forest-dwelling bird found along Canada’s Pacific coast. In Canada, it is primarily found in British Columbia, where it inhabits coastal and interior mountain forests from Vancouver Island to the mainland ranges. These non-migratory birds are best known for their distinctive spring courtship displays.
SPELT: Spelt is one of the world’s oldest cultivated grains and is still grown on Canadian farms today. This heritage wheat variety is known for its distinctive nutty flavour and is prized by artisan bakers for creating traditional breads, pastas, and other specialty foods. As part of Canada’s rich grain-growing tradition, spelt joins a diverse agricultural industry that makes Canada one of the world’s leading grain exporters.
SPICE: Emerging spice crops in Saskatchewan include coriander, caraway, dill, anise, and fenugreek, but mustard seed is the most important spice crop in Saskatchewan. Canada is the second largest producer in the world with over 200,000 tonnes per year, and the largest exporter with 160,000 tonnes per year. Saskatchewan produces 80–90% of the Canadian mustard seed and is known worldwide for the production of a high-quality product.
SPILE: A spile is a tube mechanism that you tap into a tree to collect sap, which in turn can be evaporated and boiled for delicious maple syrup!
SQUAB: A squab is a young pigeon, once raised on Canadian farms as a delicacy for its tender meat. In the late 1800s and early 1900s, squab was served in hotels and dining halls across the country. While today pigeons are more often spotted on city streets and town squares, the word squab offers a glimpse into Canada’s rich farming and culinary traditions.
SQUIB: In the world of film and TV production, a squib is a small, controlled explosion used to simulate bullet hits or sudden impact – often seen in action movies. Canada, particularly Vancouver (a.k.a. Hollywood North) and Toronto, is a global hub for filming, and many productions here rely on Canadian special effects artists to rig squibs for dramatic scenes. If you've watched series like The Boys, Reacher, or even older hits like X-Men, chances are you've seen squib effects made and managed by Canadian crews.
START: In 2025, [Canadian Tire’s Jumpstart program](https://jumpstart.canadiantire.ca/) celebrates 20 years of helping kids across Canada start their journey in sports by removing financial barriers. Since 2005, Jumpstart has provided funding for equipment, registration fees, and transportation so thousands of children can get active, build confidence, and feel part of their communities. Getting a great start in sports helps kids grow stronger – on the field and off.
STATE: Canada's political system is based on that of the United Kingdom. It is a constitutional monarchy, which means that we recognize the Queen or King as the Head of State, while the Prime Minister is the Head of Government. Currently, His Majesty King Charles III is King of Canada and Canada's Head of State. He is the personal embodiment of the Crown in Canada. A state funeral for former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney is being held today in Montreal. Wayne Gretzky will be among the high-profile figures to eulogize the former PM. Mulroney passed away on Feb 29, 2024 at the age of 84. He served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993.
STEEL: Steel plays an extremely important role in the Canadian economy as a whole: in 2019, the Canadian steel industry contributed $4.2 billion to Canada's GDP. According to the Canadian Steel Producers Association, the Canadian steel industry employs, directly and indirectly, more than 120,000 Canadians.
STEER: At the [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/), steer wrestling is a fan-favourite event that puts cowboy courage to the test! In this thrilling rodeo challenge, a rider leaps from a galloping horse and attempts to wrestle a sprinting steer to the ground using strength, speed, and precision. It’s a heart-pounding highlight of the Stampede, showcasing the daring skills rooted in Canada’s ranching traditions.
STOAT: Stoats, also known as short-tailed weasels or ermines, are widespread across Canada. Found in most regions, they grow a white winter coat for camouflage, slipping through snow and tunnels as fearless hunters of mice, voles, birds, and insects. That same nimble, energetic spirit comes to life in [Tina and Milo](https://www.olympics.com/en/milano-cortina-2026/brand/mascots), the stoat siblings who are mascots for the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics, bringing fun, cheer, and Olympic excitement to athletes and fans alike.
STOCK: The Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) is a stock exchange located in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. It is the 10th largest exchange in the world and the third largest in North America based on market capitalization. The Montreal Exchange is Canada's oldest exchange and was formerly called the Montreal Stock Exchange.
STONY: [Stony Plain](https://www.stonyplain.com/) is a town in the Edmonton Metropolitan Region of Alberta that is situated on the traditional lands of Treaty 6 peoples. Stony Plain is known for its many painted murals representing various periods, events and people throughout the town's history. The town was originally known as Dog Rump Creek. Stony Plain is also home to [Canadian History Ehx](https://canadaehx.com/) podcaster and historian, [Craig Baird](https://x.com/CraigBaird), who explores the good, the bad and the weird of Canada's history. Join Canuckle in wishing Craig a very happy birthday today!
STOOK: A stook, also referred to as a shock or stack, is an arrangement of sheaves of cut grain-stalks placed so as to keep the grain-heads off the ground while still in the field and before collection for threshing. Stooked grain sheaves are typically wheat, barley and oats. In Canada, a stook may also refer to a field stack of small, rectangular bales of hay or straw. These bales may be stacked and deposited by a "stooking machine" or "stooker" that is dragged, sled-like, behind the baler.
STORK: The Great Stork Derby was a decade-long baby-making contest held from 1926 to 1936. Female residents of Toronto, Ontario, Canada, competed to produce the most babies in order to qualify for an unusual bequest in the will of eccentric millionaire Charles Vance Millar. In the end, there were six women tied for first place. The winners each gave birth to nine children, and received $125,000 (worth roughly $2 million today).
STORY: Winterlude 2026’s [Lantern Grove](https://www.lanterngrove.ca/) transforms Confederation Park into a magical, light-filled story-driven experience built around a winter tale of community and generosity. Produced by Immersive International and presented by [Ottawa Tourism](https://ottawatourism.ca/en/event-calendar/lantern-grove), visitors can wander among sculptural installations, dynamic lighting, whimsical sound design, and the enchanting Cinema Forest. A short film expands the story on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday evenings, making Lantern Grove feel like stepping inside a living Canadian winter story.
STYLE: Style in Canada is as diverse as the country itself – from cozy winter layers to cutting-edge couture. Canada’s fashion scene celebrates creativity and identity, with Montréal’s vibrant design houses and [Toronto’s Fashion Week](https://fashionarttoronto.ca/) runways leading the way. Brands like [Canada Goose](https://www.canadagoose.com/ca/en/home-page), [Smythe](https://shopsmythe.com/), and Indigenous-owned labels such as [Lesley Hampton](https://lesleyhampton.com/) and [Section 35](https://www.sectionthirtyfive.com/) show how Canadian style blends function, culture, and artistry – proof that true northern style never goes out of fashion!
